"Someone drills through something they were told not to drill through."

Ian paused.

"Fire them."

Ji-man laughed.

"After you update the model."

Ian crossed his arms.

"So I'm right."

"About what?"

"If we measure enough variables, the model converges toward reality."

Ji-man looked at the page for a moment.

"Toward."

Ian noticed the word.

"Not to?"

"Sometimes close enough that the difference stops mattering for the decision you're making."

"That isn't the same."

"No."

Ian waited.

Ji-man put down the pencil.

"You want the universe to provide an answer key."

"It has one."

"Does it?"

"Reality only happens one way."

Ji-man tilted his head.

"That doesn't mean you can know every reason it happened that way."

"But the reasons exist."

"Probably."

Ian heard the hesitation.

"Probably?"

His father reached for his coffee again.

"You're asking an engineer to solve philosophy before lunch."

"It's four in the afternoon."

"Then definitely no."

Ian stared at him until Ji-man gave in.

"Look."

His father tapped the foundation plan.

"I believe structures are honest."

Ian's expression changed.

That sounded closer to something he could accept.

Ji-man continued.

"Not because they are simple. Because they cannot negotiate with load."

He pointed at one of the columns.

"If this member is too weak, a committee cannot vote it stronger."

Another.

"If the load path is broken, a press release cannot reconnect it."

He looked at Ian.

"But engineers can still misunderstand why something failed."

Ian said nothing.

"That's why you don't fall in love with your first explanation."

Ji-man slid the compass back across the table.

"You fix the center."

He touched the drawing.

"You don't fix the evidence."

For several seconds, only the refrigerator and distant traffic filled the apartment.

Ian looked down at the instrument.

The center point had left a tiny hole in the paper.

Permanent.

Small enough that no one else would notice it.

Later that evening, his mother came home carrying two bags of groceries and immediately objected to the engineering occupation of the dining room.

"Ji-man."

Her husband looked up.

"Yes?"

"Why is there a building where dinner goes?"

He looked at the plans.

Then at the table.

"It was zoned commercial this afternoon."

Yoo Seo-yeon set the bags on the kitchen counter.

"It is being rezoned."

Ian began rolling the tracing paper before she could do it herself.

Seo-yeon worked in international freight coordination for an industrial trading company. She spent her days dealing with containers, manifests, insurance certificates, port schedules, customs releases, and suppliers who discovered different definitions of the word urgent depending on who was paying.

Her work did not interest Ian in the same way his father's did.

Buildings obeyed equations.

Shipping seemed to obey telephones.

Still, she possessed one skill that repeatedly defeated both Ian and Ji-man.

She remembered where things actually were.

Not where the spreadsheet claimed they were.

Where they were.

She opened the refrigerator.

"Did either of you eat?"

Ji-man pointed at the tangerine peels.

"Balanced diet."

Seo-yeon stared at him.

"I married poorly."

"You were warned."

Ian carried the rolled drawings toward the study.

His mother noticed the compass in his hand.

"That old thing?"

Ian stopped.

"It works."

"It worked when your grandfather used it."

Ji-man looked toward her.

"It still works."

Seo-yeon took a carton of eggs from a shopping bag.

"Doesn't mean you should give it to a seventeen-year-old."

Ian looked offended.

"I'm careful."

His mother raised one eyebrow.

"Last month you dismantled the rice cooker."

"It had inefficient temperature control."

"It no longer had any temperature control."

"I fixed it."

"After three days."

Ji-man rescued the compass before the argument expanded.

"He did well."

Seo-yeon looked between them.

"That's how it starts."

"How what starts?"

"Two men explaining to me why the broken object is actually an experiment."

Ian smiled despite himself.

She turned back to the groceries.

"Dinner in twenty minutes."

Ji-man glanced at the clock.

"I need to send one review note."

Seo-yeon did not turn around.

"No."

"One."

"No."

"Five minutes."

"That means forty."

Ji-man looked toward Ian for support.

Ian immediately betrayed him.

"Usually fifty."

Seo-yeon pointed at her son.

"See? One competent person in this family."

Ji-man sighed theatrically and closed his laptop.

Dinner was ordinary.

Years later, Ian would remember that more clearly than almost anything else about the evening.

His mother complaining about a shipment delayed in Busan because two database systems disagreed over the same container number.

His father insisting the problem proved software engineers should be licensed like structural engineers.

Seo-yeon telling him structural engineers could first learn to answer email before regulating anyone else.

Ian eating too quickly.

The television playing softly from the living room.

A weather presenter describing a cold front moving down the peninsula.

Nothing announced itself as important.

Nothing warned him to memorize it.

After dinner, Ji-man washed the dishes because Seo-yeon had cooked.

Ian stood beside him drying them.

"Appa."

"Hm?"

"About the Helios project."

Ji-man kept washing.

"What about it?"

"The transfer level."

"What about it?"

"You don't like it."

The movement of the sponge slowed slightly.

Ian noticed.

"I didn't say that."

"You kept checking the same load path."

Ji-man rinsed a plate.

"That is what reviewing means."

"You checked it four times."

His father handed him the plate.

"You counted?"

"Yes."

"That's unsettling."

"Is something wrong with it?"

Ji-man turned off the tap.

For a moment he looked toward the dining table, where the rolled drawings rested beside his closed laptop.

"Not wrong."

Ian waited.

"Uncomfortable."

"What does that mean?"

"It means the design works if several assumptions remain true."

"Which assumptions?"

"Construction sequence. Boundary stiffness. Load redistribution at the podium."

"So check them."

"I am."

"And?"

Ji-man dried his hands.

"And people get irritated when the reviewer asks the same question after everyone else wants the answer to be finished."

Ian felt the first trace of something he could not name.

"Do you think it's unsafe?"

Ji-man considered the question seriously.

"No."

Ian relaxed.

Then his father added:

"I think parts of the argument are weaker than the confidence people are placing in them."

Ian frowned.

"That's almost the same thing."

"No."

"It sounds the same."

"It isn't."

Ji-man leaned against the counter.

"Engineering has a bad habit. When enough people repeat that a risk has been addressed, the sentence begins to sound like evidence."

Ian thought about that.

"So you don't trust them."

"Trust is not the variable."

"What is?"

"Can the assumptions be verified?"

There it was again.

Not belief.

Verification.

Ji-man took the towel from Ian and hung it on the cabinet handle.

"If they can, good."

"And if they can't?"

"Then you say so in writing."

"Even if they don't like it."

"Especially then."

Ian looked toward the compass lying on the dining table.

"Don't move the center."

Ji-man smiled.

"Exactly."

That night, Ian sat at his desk beneath the narrow window of his bedroom.

The city outside had disappeared into darkness and reflected apartment light. His physics homework remained open but unfinished.

Beside it lay the compass.

His father had forgotten to take it back.

Or perhaps he had left it intentionally.

Ian opened the legs and placed the needle against a page of graph paper.

He drew a circle.

Then another around it.

Then a third.

Each shared the same center.

The pattern pleased him.

One fixed point.

Different boundaries.

No ambiguity about where any of them began.

His phone vibrated.

A message from his father, sent from the living room despite being less than ten meters away.

Don't stab the desk. Your mother will blame me.

Ian typed:

The desk has measurable tolerance.

Three dots appeared.

Then:

That sentence is why people avoid engineers at parties.

Ian almost laughed.

He placed the phone face down.

The compass remained open beneath his fingers.

Beyond his room, his parents were arguing gently about whether the bedroom heating was too high. Somewhere outside, a motorcycle accelerated between apartment blocks. A plane crossed the dark sky toward Gimpo, its red navigation light appearing and disappearing behind thin cloud.

Ian pressed the point down again.

The center held.

He rotated the graphite leg around it until the line returned cleanly to its beginning.

At seventeen, he still believed that was what his father had taught him.

Choose the center carefully.

Then refuse to move it.

### [Scene 2: The Collapse]

The first warning was a vibration nobody on the street understood.

At 14:17 on a Wednesday afternoon, three security cameras mounted along the western edge of the Helios complex recorded a subtle shiver passing through the lower facade of the central tower.

It lasted less than two seconds.

Pedestrians did not stop.

Traffic continued through the intersection.

Inside the ground-floor retail concourse, suspended signs moved slightly on their cables. A barista steadied a stack of paper cups with one hand and looked toward the ceiling.

The vibration stopped.

Thirty-one seconds later, one of the tower's lower transfer levels failed.

Not explosively.

Not all at once.

A deep metallic report traveled through the structure, followed by a series of shorter impacts that seemed to descend through the building faster than anyone inside could understand.

The tower moved.

Then the city began to run.

Ian was in physics class when the emergency alert reached every phone in the room at once.

The sound was immediate and ugly: thirty identical electronic alarms breaking across the teacher's voice.

Students reached into pockets.

The teacher frowned.

"Phones down."

Nobody listened.

Ian looked at his screen.

EMERGENCY SAFETY ALERT

STRUCTURAL INCIDENT — GANGNAM DISTRICT

AVOID HELIOS REDEVELOPMENT AREA

For a second, the name did not mean anything.

Then it did.

Ian stood so quickly his chair struck the desk behind him.

The teacher looked at him.

"Ian."

He was already calling his father.

The line rang.

Once.

Twice.

Three times.

No answer.

He called again.

Nothing.

His mother.

Seo-yeon answered on the second ring.

"Ian?"

"Where's Appa?"

A pause.

Too long.

"I'm calling him."

"He isn't answering."

"I know."

Her voice had changed.

Not panic.

Concentration.

Ian knew that voice. She used it when shipments vanished between two ports and everyone else started guessing.

"Are you at school?"

"Yes."

"Stay there."

"Umma—"

"Stay there."

The call ended.

Ian looked at the emergency alert again.

The room around him had changed. Several students were already watching live video.

Someone turned up the volume.

A shaky phone camera showed the Helios tower behind a row of buses and emergency vehicles.

The upper structure was still standing.

The lower podium was not.

A dense cloud of gray dust rolled across the avenue.

People were running toward the camera.

The video shook violently.

Then the tower disappeared behind the dust.

Ian moved closer without realizing it.

"What happened?" someone asked.

Nobody answered.

Another student refreshed a news feed.

A headline appeared before any reporter could possibly have known enough to write one.

PARTIAL COLLAPSE AT HELIOS COMPLEX — CASUALTIES FEARED

Ian called his father again.

No answer.

The teacher stepped toward him.

"You need to sit down."

Ian looked at the live image.

The tower emerged through the dust.

Still standing.

But wrong.

A section of the lower western facade had folded inward. Several floors above the podium no longer aligned cleanly with the vertical grid. One corner appeared to have dropped farther than the others.

Ian felt something cold move through his chest.

He had seen that load path on the dining table.

He knew the drawing.

Not the building.

The drawing.

His father had traced those columns with one finger.

The line disappears because the load changes path.

Ian enlarged the image.

The failure was not where he remembered the weakest part of the argument.

At least, he did not think it was.

He called again.

No answer.

Seo-yeon arrived at the school nineteen minutes later.

She did not park.

The car stopped half across the curb.

Ian climbed into the passenger seat before she could tell him to hurry.

"Hospital?"

"No."

"Helios?"

"No."

"Then where?"

"Home."

"Why?"

She pulled away from the curb.

"Because I need his files."

Ian stared at her.

"The building collapsed."

"I know."

"Then why are we going home?"

"Because your father wasn't at Helios."

Ian stopped breathing for a moment.

"What?"

Seo-yeon kept her eyes on the road.

"He was supposed to be."

"Supposed to?"

"He left the office this morning."

"For Helios?"

"That's what he told me."

"So he's there."

"No."

"How do you know?"

She gripped the steering wheel harder.

"Because his office called me."

Ian waited.

"They said two government investigators came for him before lunch."

The city outside continued normally.

That was the part Ian would remember.

Traffic lights changed.

A delivery scooter passed between lanes.

A woman stood beneath a bus shelter holding a red umbrella.

The world had not yet decided that his life had changed.

"What investigators?"

"They didn't know."

"Police?"

"They said government."

"What does that mean?"

"I don't know."

"Why would they take him?"

"I don't know."

The answer came sharply.

Seo-yeon glanced at him.

"I know what I know. I don't know the rest."

Ian looked back at his phone.

Live footage showed emergency crews moving through the Helios plaza.

"How long ago?"

"His office thinks around ten."

Ian looked at the dashboard clock.

14:44.

More than four hours.

"He was taken four hours before the collapse."

Seo-yeon said nothing.

Ian repeated it.

"Four hours."

"I heard you."

"That's before anything happened."

"Yes."

"Then why—"

"I don't know."

This time she said it more quietly.

Ian stared out the window.

The city blurred past.

His father's unanswered call log filled the screen.

At home, the dining table was empty.

No tracing paper.

No structural plans.

No laptop.

Seo-yeon walked directly into the study.

Ian followed.

The room looked wrong before he understood why.

One shelf stood slightly open.

A drawer had not been pushed all the way back into the desk.

A stack of notebooks had been moved.

Not thrown.

Moved.

Precisely enough that another person might not have noticed.

Ian did.

His father aligned things.

The office had been searched.

Seo-yeon opened the desk drawers one by one.

"His work laptop is gone."

Ian looked toward the shelf.

"The Helios drawings?"

"Gone."

"They were here."

"I know."

She checked the small fireproof cabinet beneath the desk.

Unlocked.

Empty.

Ian stood in the center of the room.

"Did they come here too?"

Seo-yeon looked around.

Then at the apartment door.

"No damage."

"They had a key?"

"Or I left it unlocked."

"You never leave it unlocked."

"I know."

Ian's eyes moved across the room.

Nothing was broken.

That made it worse.

His father's absence had been organized.

Seo-yeon reached for her phone.

"Who are you calling?"

"His office again."

Ian opened his father's desk computer.

The monitor came alive.

Password screen.

He knew the password.

Or thought he did.

It failed.

Again.

Failed.

"Appa changed it."

Seo-yeon stopped dialing.

"When?"

"I don't know."

"Try his old work phrase."

Ian did.

Failed.

The machine locked for thirty seconds.

Seo-yeon stared at the screen.

Then she said:

"Stop."

"Why?"

"Because if somebody changed it remotely, I don't want you generating an access log."

Ian looked at her.

She was already thinking differently.

Not about what the computer contained.

About who could see them touching it.

A news alert appeared on her phone.

She read it.

Her face changed.

"What?"

She turned the screen toward Ian.

AUTHORITIES INVESTIGATING POSSIBLE EXPLOSIVE RESIDUE AT HELIOS SITE

Ian read the line twice.

"Explosive?"

"It says possible residue."

"From what?"

"It doesn't say."

Another alert arrived.

Then another.

Television networks had begun repeating the same words.

Possible explosive residue.

Security investigation.

Structural sabotage not ruled out.

Ian looked back toward the study.

"My father was taken before the building collapsed."

Seo-yeon did not answer.

"And now they're saying explosives."

"Ian."

"He reviewed the structure."

"I know."

"They took his files."

"I know."

"Before the collapse."

"I know."

"Then they already knew."

Seo-yeon turned on him.

"No."

The word was hard enough to stop him.

"You do not know that."

"They took him four hours before—"

"That proves they took him four hours before."

"Why else?"

"I don't know."

"There has to be a reason."

"There is."

"Then—"

"That does not mean you know which one."

Ian stared at her.

Seo-yeon stepped closer.

"Listen to me."

Her voice lowered.

"This is where people start destroying their own judgment."

Ian said nothing.

"Something is wrong. Maybe several things. But you do not fill the empty spaces because the pattern frightens you."

He looked toward the television.

The same video loop played again.

Dust.

Sirens.

The lower tower folding inward.

"Then what do we do?"

Seo-yeon looked at the study.

"We separate what happened from what people say happened."

By sunset, the official casualty estimate had risen above three hundred.

By midnight, it exceeded five hundred.

The tower itself remained partially standing, but much of the lower complex had pancaked through several occupied levels. Rescue crews worked under floodlights while drones circled the surviving structure.

Helicopter footage revealed more than the phone videos had.

The failure had begun near the lower transfer region.

One portion of the podium had dropped sharply.

The tower above it had rotated slightly and settled asymmetrically.

Ian sat less than a meter from the television.

He had not changed out of his school uniform.

Seo-yeon was in the kitchen making calls.

He barely heard her.

On the screen, a structural engineer from a university stood beside a simplified graphic.

"At this stage," the expert said, "it would be irresponsible to speculate about a precise initiating mechanism. What we can say is that the collapse appears to involve progressive loss of load-transfer capacity in the lower structure."

Ian leaned closer.

The graphic was crude.

But the language mattered.

Progressive loss.

Transfer structure.

He remembered his father at the table.

The design works if several assumptions remain true.

Construction sequence.

Boundary stiffness.

Load redistribution.

Ian opened a notebook.

He drew the lower portion of the tower from memory.

Not accurately.

Enough.

He marked the transfer level.

Then the apparent initiation zone visible in the helicopter footage.

The locations did not match the area his father had been most concerned about.

Ian stopped.

That should have reassured him.

It didn't.

Because if the suspected weak load path had not initiated the collapse, then the simple explanation forming in his head was already wrong.

His father had been worried.

But perhaps not about the thing that failed.

The front door opened.

Ian stood.

Not his father.

Two police officers entered first.

Behind them stood three men in dark civilian coats.

Seo-yeon came from the kitchen.

"Who are you?"

One of the police officers showed identification.

"Mrs. Yoo Seo-yeon?"

"Yes."

"We have a warrant to conduct an additional search related to the Helios investigation."

"Additional?"

One of the civilian men looked at the study.

Seo-yeon saw it.

"You were already here."

No answer.

"Before the collapse?"

The senior officer kept his voice neutral.

"Ma'am, I need you to step aside."

"You entered my home before this?"

"We are executing a lawful search."

"What happened to my husband?"

"I don't have information I can provide."

"Where is he?"

"I don't know."

"Who does?"

The officer did not answer.

One of the men in civilian clothes entered the study.

Ian moved toward him.

"Don't touch that."

The man turned.

Seo-yeon caught Ian's arm.

"Ian."

"That's my father's computer."

"I know."

The man unplugged it.

Ian tried to move again.

His mother's grip tightened.

"Don't."

He looked at her.

She wasn't afraid of the man.

She was afraid of what Ian would do.

The officers collected the desktop computer.

Two external drives.

A box of handwritten notebooks.

Several project folders.

A tablet.

The old office printer's internal storage module.

They photographed every shelf.

They bagged loose papers.

Nothing was hurried.

Nothing was improvised.

This search had a list.

Ian watched each item disappear.

One of the civilian investigators approached the dining table.

The silver drafting compass lay beside Ian's unfinished physics homework.

The man picked it up.

Ian's body moved before thought.

"That's mine."

The investigator looked at him.

"It's a drafting compass."

"It isn't work material."

"Was it used by your father?"

"Yes."

The investigator placed it inside a clear evidence bag.

Ian stepped forward.

Seo-yeon released his arm.

"This is not relevant to your warrant," she said.

The investigator looked at her.

"It was in the residence and belonged to the subject."

"My husband is not a subject."

The investigator did not respond.

Seo-yeon held out her hand.

"Show me the section authorizing seizure of personal family property unrelated to Helios."

A pause.

The senior police officer came over.

He read the warrant.

Then looked at the bag.

"Leave it."

The civilian investigator hesitated.

"Officer—"

"Leave it."

The compass returned to the table.

The bag remained empty.

Ian stared at it.

A few minutes later, the search team left with the computers and papers.

The apartment door closed.

Silence returned.

Seo-yeon locked it.

Then the chain.

Then she checked the lock twice.

Ian went to the table.

He picked up the compass.

The metal was still warm from another man's hand.

At 02:13, a structural animation appeared on a major national network.

The graphic showed an explosive event near the lower transfer structure followed by cascading column failure.

The presenter emphasized that the animation was preliminary.

Ian watched it three times.

On the fourth, he paused the recording.

His father had once shown him what a progressive asymmetric transfer failure should look like.

Not this exact building.

Not this exact event.

But the logic.

Load leaves one support.

Neighboring members inherit it.

Deflection grows.

Connections fail in sequence.

The structure searches for another path until none remains.

The animation on television showed something cleaner.

Too clean, Ian thought.

Then he caught himself.

He had no data.

Only video.

He opened his notebook.

At the top of a fresh page, he wrote:

WHAT I KNOW

Appa left his office in the morning.

Government investigators took him before noon.

Helios collapsed at 14:17.

Investigators had already searched the apartment before we returned.

Officials are investigating possible explosive residue.

Appa's Helios records were seized.

He stopped.

Then below it:

WHAT I THINK

The timing is connected.

Appa knew something.

The collapse did not look like the failure he described.

He stared at the two lists.

The first felt solid.

The second did not.

His mother entered the room.

She had changed into a sweater but had not slept.

She read the page over his shoulder.

"Good."

Ian looked at her.

"What?"

"The separation."

She pointed at the headings.

"Keep doing that."

He looked back at the television.

"What if the second list is right?"

"Then evidence will move things from the second list to the first."

"And if there's no evidence?"

"Then you don't get to move them."

Ian frowned.

"Even if it's obvious?"

"Especially if it's obvious."

She sat beside him.

For a long time neither spoke.

On the television, rescue lights moved across the broken lower floors of Helios.

"Umma."

"Yes?"

"Do you think Appa did something?"

Seo-yeon turned toward him.

"No."

He looked at her.

"You answered fast."

"I know your father."

"That's not evidence."

Something painful moved across her face.

"No."

Ian waited.

She looked back at the screen.

"But it is enough for me to keep looking."

At 03:41, Ian's phone rang.

Unknown number.

He answered immediately.

"Hello?"

Silence.

Then breathing.

"Ian?"

His father's voice.

Ian stood so fast the chair fell backward.

"Appa?"

Seo-yeon was beside him instantly.

Ian switched to speaker.

"Where are you?"

A pause.

Static.

"I can't talk long."

Seo-yeon leaned toward the phone.

"Ji-man. Where are you?"

Another pause.

"They're moving me."

"Who?"

No answer.

"Ji-man?"

His breathing was uneven.

Not panicked.

Controlled.

Ian recognized that too.

His father sounded like he did when calculating something while everyone else spoke.

"Listen to me," Ji-man said.

Both of them went silent.

"The tower didn't fail the way they think it did."

Ian stopped breathing.

Seo-yeon closed her eyes.

"What do you mean?" Ian asked.

"I don't know yet."

"Was it explosives?"

"Ian."

"Was it?"

"I don't know."

"Then what happened?"

"I don't know."

The words came faster now.

"But the transfer response isn't consistent with the sequence they showed me."

"Who showed you?"

No answer.

"Appa, who?"

The line crackled.

Ji-man continued.

"The lower structure should have redistributed asymmetrically before global loss. That's not what the preliminary sensor sequence indicates."

Ian grabbed his notebook.

"What does it indicate?"

"I don't have enough."

"Tell me anyway."

"No."

"Why?"

"Because you will mistake an incomplete pattern for an answer."

Ian froze.

His father continued.

"Don't do that."

Seo-yeon leaned closer.

"Ji-man, are you under arrest?"

A pause.

"I haven't been formally charged."

"Then why can't you come home?"

No answer.

"Who has you?"

Still nothing.

"Ji-man."

His voice returned softer.

"Seo-yeon."

She closed her eyes.

"Take Ian somewhere else tonight."

Her face changed.

"Why?"

"I don't know."

"Stop saying that."

"I mean it."

Silence.

"Something is wrong with the timeline."

Ian looked down at his notebook.

The phrase entered him differently from everything else his father had said.

Not the structure.

The timeline.

"What timeline?" Ian asked.

The connection degraded.

"Ian."

"Yes."

"Remember the compass?"

Ian looked at it on the table.

"Yes."

"Keep the center fixed."

The line crackled.

"But don't confuse the center with the answer."

Ian frowned.

"What does that mean?"

No response.

"Appa?"

A final burst of static.

Then Ji-man's voice, barely audible.

"Check what actually happened."

The call ended.

Ian stared at the phone.

Call duration:

01:47

No location.

No caller identification.

Nothing he could use.

Seo-yeon was already moving.

She took two travel bags from the closet.

Ian watched her.

"Where are we going?"

"I don't know yet."

"Appa said—"

"I heard him."

She opened the first bag.

"Pack clothes. Two days."

Ian didn't move.

"Now."

He looked once more at the television.

Helios remained frozen on the screen.

A broken building under floodlights.

The official animation sat paused beside it.

One structure.

Two explanations.

Neither complete.

Ian picked up the silver compass and closed its legs.

He placed it in his pocket.

At seventeen, he still believed the problem was simply finding the correct center.

He had not yet learned what people would do to make a center disappear.


## Chapter 1: The Architectural Flaw

### [Scene 1: The Raid]

By 05:12, the apartment no longer looked inhabited.

Seo-yeon packed with the efficiency of someone accustomed to missed connections.

Two changes of clothes each.

Passports.

Medication.

Cash.

Phone chargers.

A small external battery.

No framed photographs.

No books.

Nothing that could not be abandoned.

Ian stood in the doorway of his room holding his school backpack.

"Where are we going?"

Seo-yeon zipped the first bag.

"My sister's."

"In Ilsan?"

"For now."

"Appa said somewhere else."

"He said somewhere else tonight."

"It's already morning."

She looked at him.

"This is still tonight."

Ian did not argue.

He put the compass into the inner pocket of his backpack.

Then removed it.

He slipped it into the pocket of his jacket instead.

Closer.

Seo-yeon noticed but said nothing.

Before leaving, she walked through the apartment once more.

Windows locked.

Gas off.

Study door open.

Nothing hidden.

At the front entrance she paused.

Ian expected her to check the lock.

Instead she took out her phone and photographed the apartment from the doorway.

"What are you doing?"

"Recording how we left it."

"For what?"

"So later I don't have to remember."

She took another photograph showing the time on the wall clock.

05:18.

Ian watched her.

His mother had spent years arguing with freight forwarders about damaged containers, missing seals, and cargo that was somehow always intact until responsibility changed hands.

He had once thought her habit of photographing everything was excessive.

Now he understood it differently.

Memory could argue.

A timestamp could be checked.

They left.

The streets were almost empty.

Seoul before sunrise had none of the confidence it displayed during the day. Delivery trucks occupied lanes usually filled with sedans. Convenience stores glowed at intersections. Municipal cleaning crews moved beneath fluorescent jackets while the skyline remained a dark geometry of towers against a slowly whitening sky.

Seo-yeon did not take the direct route toward Ilsan.

Ian noticed after six minutes.

"Wrong way."

"I know."

"Why?"

She changed lanes.

"Your father told us to leave."

"That doesn't mean we're being followed."

"No."

"Do you think we are?"

"I don't know."

Ian looked through the rear window.

Two taxis.

A refrigerated truck.

A black sedan three vehicles back.

He watched it through two intersections.

It turned away.

"Then why change routes?"

"Because finding out costs almost nothing."

That sounded like her.

Not suspicion.

Verification.

Seo-yeon crossed the river, drove east for several kilometers, then doubled back through a surface road before joining the expressway north.

No vehicle stayed with them.

Ian relaxed slightly.

His mother did not.

At 05:43 her phone rang.

Her sister.

Seo-yeon answered through the car speakers.

"Unni?"

The reply came immediately.

"Don't come."

Seo-yeon's hands tightened on the wheel.

"Why?"

"There are police here."

Ian turned toward her.

"At your apartment?"

"No. Downstairs. Two cars. They asked the security desk whether you were coming."

Seo-yeon said nothing.

Her sister's voice dropped.

"They showed your photo."

"Did they say why?"

"They said they needed to speak with you in connection with Ji-man."

"Police?"

"I saw police identification. There were other people."

"What people?"

"Suits. I don't know."

Seo-yeon glanced at Ian.

"Did they enter your apartment?"

"No."

"Did they ask to?"

"Not yet."

"Don't let them without paperwork."

"Seo-yeon, what is happening?"

"I don't know."

"Is Ji-man involved in this explosion thing?"

Ian saw his mother flinch.

"Don't say that."

"It's all over the news."

"I know what's on the news."

"Then tell me what—"

"I can't."

A long silence.

Her sister spoke again.

"Where are you?"

Seo-yeon looked at the navigation screen.

Then switched it off.

"Not coming to you."

She ended the call.

For several seconds, the only sound inside the car was tire noise.

Ian looked ahead.

"So they expected us there."

"Maybe."

"How would they know?"

"Family address records. Phone records. Basic investigation."

"They got there before us."

"Yes."

"Like Appa."

Seo-yeon turned toward him briefly.

"Don't build the conclusion yet."

"They're always first."

"That is still not a conclusion."

Ian looked away.

It was beginning to feel like one.

They stopped at a twenty-four-hour rest area outside the city.

Seo-yeon parked beneath a row of sodium lamps far from the main building.

"Leave your phone."

Ian looked at her.

"Why?"

"Because I want ten minutes in which I know what device is reporting our location."

"Phones don't constantly report exact location to random people."

"I didn't say random people."

She powered hers down.

Ian did the same.

They entered the rest area carrying only her wallet and his backpack.

Inside, a television above the convenience-store counter showed Helios.

The headline had changed.

NATIONAL SECURITY AUTHORITIES JOIN HELIOS SABOTAGE INVESTIGATION

A reporter stood behind a police cordon.

"...officials have not confirmed the identity of any suspects, but investigators are examining whether explosive material may have been introduced during construction or maintenance. Sources familiar with the inquiry say national-security agencies are now participating alongside police and fire authorities."

Ian stopped beneath the screen.

The report cut to footage of his father's engineering firm.

Three dark vans were parked outside.

Uniformed police controlled the entrance.

Men and women wearing evidence vests carried sealed boxes from the building.

Ian stepped closer.

"That's Appa's office."

Seo-yeon followed his gaze.

The camera zoomed in.

A reporter continued.

"Authorities are executing multiple search warrants this morning against firms and individuals associated with the tower's structural review, construction management, and materials supply chain."

Not only Ji-man.

Ian heard the distinction.

Several companies.

Multiple individuals.

A broad investigation.

For a moment, that weakened the pattern forming in his head.

Then the camera showed one of the seized boxes.

The side of it carried his father's consulting firm's logo.

Ian looked at the clock on the television.

06:08.

Less than sixteen hours after the collapse.

"That's fast."

Seo-yeon nodded.

"It is."

"Too fast?"

"I don't know."

He hated how often she said that now.

"So what would be normal?"

"For an accident this large? Police, fire, structural safety teams immediately. Search warrants can move fast if there is a national-security basis."

"Explosives."

"If they actually have preliminary residue data."

"If."

"Yes."

Ian looked at her.

"Do you believe them?"

Seo-yeon watched the screen.

"I believe they are acting as if they believe something."

"That's not the same."

"No."

The reporter continued.

"...a joint investigative team led by the National Police Agency is coordinating with the National Intelligence Service on potential national-security aspects. Officials emphasized that no final determination has been made regarding terrorism or sabotage."

Seo-yeon pointed at the screen.

"Remember that."

"What?"

"The police are executing the criminal warrants. NIS is coordinating intelligence."

Ian frowned.

"Why does that matter?"

"Because if you're going to accuse an institution of doing something, first know which institution is legally doing what."

Even now, she corrected categories.

Ian looked back at the raid.

People carried his father's work out in numbered evidence bags.

At 06:31, Seo-yeon borrowed the rest area's public telephone.

Ian stood close enough to hear only her side.

"Yes. Yoo Seo-yeon."

Pause.

"Kim Ji-man's spouse."

Pause.

"I need to know where he is being held."

Longer pause.

"No. He called us at 03:41."

She listened.

"Then somebody has a record."

Another pause.

"No, I am not giving you our current location."

Her shoulders tightened.

"Because you called my sister before you called me."

Silence.

"Which agency?"

She reached into her bag and pulled out a pen.

"Name again."

She wrote on a paper receipt.

"National Police Agency Joint Investigation Team."

Another line.

"Is he under arrest?"

Pause.

"What does 'protective investigative custody' mean?"

Ian looked at her.

Her face changed.

"Has he been charged?"

Pause.

"Then on what authority are you restricting his movement?"

She listened for nearly twenty seconds.

"I want counsel present before any further questioning."

Pause.

"No."

Another pause.

"No, I will not bring my son to an interview."

Her eyes moved toward Ian.

"No."

She hung up.

Ian waited.

"Where is he?"

"They wouldn't say."

"Why?"

"They say his location is restricted for security reasons."

"Is he arrested?"

"They say no formal arrest has been registered."

"Then he can leave."

"Not necessarily."

"How?"

Seo-yeon looked at the receipt.

"They're claiming temporary investigative authority under the national-security inquiry while they verify his status."

"That sounds fake."

"It sounds vague."

"Same thing."

"No."

She folded the receipt and put it into her wallet.

"Vague can hide something legitimate. Or something illegitimate. We don't know which yet."

Ian looked toward the television.

"Can they keep him without charging him?"

"Not indefinitely."

"How long?"

"Long enough that I want a lawyer."

The lawyer arrived forty-eight minutes later.

His name was Han Min-seok, and he had represented Seo-yeon's employer in a customs-seizure dispute three years earlier.

He was not a criminal-defense specialist.

He had, however, answered his phone at 05:57.

That made him useful.

They met inside a rented conference room attached to a business hotel near Gimpo Airport.

Min-seok entered carrying a laptop bag and two coffees.

He did not shake hands.

"What have you told anyone?"

Seo-yeon answered.

"Only that Ji-man called at 03:41 and that I want counsel before questioning."

"Good."

He looked at Ian.

"You?"

"Nothing."

"Media?"

"No."

"Friends?"

"No."

"School?"

"No."

Min-seok sat.

"Keep it that way."

Ian disliked him immediately.

Not because he seemed dishonest.

Because he spoke as though silence were a physical tool.

Min-seok opened his laptop.

"I've confirmed there is a joint investigation. Criminal authority is being exercised by police and prosecutors. NIS is involved on the intelligence side because of the suspected explosive residue and potential foreign-security angle."

"Foreign?" Seo-yeon asked.

"That's what they're examining. I don't know whether they have evidence."

"Where is my husband?"

"I've made three requests. No confirmation yet."

"Can they do that?"

"Not for long."

"Was he arrested yesterday morning?"

"No booking record I can find."

Ian spoke.

"Then who took him from his office?"

Min-seok looked at him.

"Two investigators accompanied by police personnel, according to the office manager."

"Which investigators?"

"Unknown."

"They took him four hours before the building collapsed."

Min-seok paused.

"Approximately four hours, yes."

"Why?"

"I don't know."

Ian leaned forward.

"Doesn't that matter?"

"Very much."

"Then why is everyone talking about explosives instead?"

"Because five hundred people are dead."

The number silenced the room.

Min-seok continued.

"If authorities had intelligence about a possible threat before the collapse, your father could have been picked up because they believed he knew something. That does not mean they caused the collapse."

"I didn't say they did."

"You were going to."

Ian said nothing.

Min-seok looked toward Seo-yeon.

"This is important. There are at least three possibilities we have to keep open."

He held up one finger.

"First: your husband was already part of an unrelated national-security investigation."

Second.

"Second: authorities had advance intelligence concerning Helios and detained people associated with the structure before the event."

Third.

"Third: there is some procedural irregularity or misconduct we do not yet understand."

He lowered his hand.

"Those are not equivalent."

Ian asked:

"Which do you think?"

"I don't get paid to think before I have documents."

Seo-yeon almost smiled.

Ian did not.

At 07:26, Min-seok's phone rang.

He answered.

His expression changed halfway through the call.

"Where?"

Pause.

"When?"

He began typing.

"Was he conscious?"

Seo-yeon stood.

Min-seok raised a hand.

"Which facility?"

He listened.

"Can counsel attend?"

Pause.

"No, that's unacceptable."

Another pause.

"Put that in writing."

He ended the call.

Seo-yeon's voice was quiet.

"What?"

Min-seok closed his laptop.

"Your husband has been transferred."

"Where?"

"They won't disclose the final location."

"Transferred from where?"

"A police-affiliated secure interview facility in Seoul."

Ian stood.

"So they had him."

"Yes."

"Since when?"

"They won't tell me."

"Why was he transferred?"

"Because the investigation has been reclassified."

"As what?"

Min-seok hesitated.

"Potential terrorism."

Seo-yeon stared at him.

Ian felt the room narrow.

"Based on what?"

"Preliminary explosive-residue analysis and materials they say were recovered from several associated properties."

"Which properties?"

"No list yet."

"Our home?"

"I don't know."

Ian remembered the evidence bags.

The computers.

The notebooks.

The man reaching for the compass.

"What materials?"

"They did not specify."

Min-seok stood.

"I'm filing an emergency access request."

Seo-yeon did not move.

"Can we see him?"

"Not yet."

"Can he call?"

"I'll demand it."

"Can they move him without telling me where?"

"Temporarily under security procedures, perhaps. Without documenting it to counsel for an extended period? That becomes a much larger problem."

Ian looked at the lawyer.

"What should we do?"

Min-seok gave him the first answer that sounded useful.

"Write down everything."

Seo-yeon looked at him.

"Everything?"

"Every call. Every time. Every name. Who said what. Who refused what. Don't reconstruct later."

Ian thought of his mother's photograph at the apartment door.

05:18.

The clock visible.

He understood.

Min-seok continued.

"People remember stories. Courts need sequences."

At 08:10, Seo-yeon bought two paper notebooks from the hotel business center.

One for herself.

One for Ian.

On the first page she wrote:

KNOWN EVENTS

Beneath it:

10:04–10:20 approx. — Ji-man removed from office by investigators. Exact time unconfirmed.

14:17 — Helios structural failure begins.

~14:44 — office informs Seo-yeon Ji-man was taken before noon.

Before 14:44 — apartment appears previously searched.

Evening — formal police-led search with civilian investigators.

03:41 — phone call from Ji-man. Duration 1:47.

~05:43 — police waiting near sister's residence.

06:08 — coordinated search of Ji-man's consulting office televised.

07:26 — counsel informed Ji-man transferred under terrorism classification.

She drew a horizontal line.

Below it:

UNCONFIRMED

explosive residue

reason for Ji-man's initial detention

identity of first investigators

exact detention location

basis for terrorism designation

materials allegedly seized

Ian read the list.

"Shouldn't 'Appa didn't cause the collapse' be under known?"

Seo-yeon's pen stopped.

For several seconds, she did not answer.

Ian regretted asking.

Then she said:

"Not in this notebook."

He stared at her.

She looked directly at him.

"I believe your father."

"That's not what I asked."

"I know."

Her voice was steady.

"This notebook is not for what I believe."

Ian looked down at the page.

That hurt more than he expected.

But he understood.

Seo-yeon pushed the second notebook toward him.

"Make your own."

Ian opened it.

He wrote the same two headings.

KNOWN

UNCONFIRMED

Under KNOWN:

Appa was taken before Helios collapsed.

He stopped.

Then added:

The official investigation became terrorism-related after the collapse.

He considered another sentence.

They knew beforehand.

His pen hovered.

Then he moved it under:

UNCONFIRMED

The distinction annoyed him.

He left it there.

At 09:02, someone knocked on the conference-room door.

Three knocks.

Pause.

Two more.

Min-seok, who had returned ten minutes earlier, looked toward Seo-yeon.

"Expecting anyone?"

"No."

He approached the door but did not open it.

"Who is it?"

"National Police Agency."

Min-seok looked through the viewer.

Two uniformed officers.

Three civilian investigators.

The same configuration as the apartment.

"Do you have a warrant?"

A voice from outside answered.

"We have an order to interview Mrs. Yoo and secure digital devices relevant to the Helios investigation."

"Slide it under."

A document appeared beneath the door.

Min-seok picked it up.

Read.

His expression tightened.

"Valid?"

Seo-yeon asked.

"For device seizure, yes. Interview is voluntary unless they issue something further."

Ian stood.

"How did they find us?"

Nobody answered.

Min-seok opened the door.

The officers entered first.

The civilian investigators followed.

One introduced himself.

"Chief Inspector Park Seong-ho. Joint Investigation Team."

He showed identification.

Min-seok examined it.

Park looked toward Seo-yeon.

"Mrs. Yoo, we need your cooperation."

"You have my lawyer."

"We are aware."

Park's eyes moved to Ian.

"And your son."

"He's seventeen."

"We are not here to question him without a guardian."

Seo-yeon stepped slightly between them anyway.

Park placed a document on the table.

"We are authorized to secure devices belonging to your husband and any devices that may contain communications related to Helios."

"You already took our computers," Ian said.

Park looked at him.

"Some."

"You took everything."

Park did not respond.

Two digital-forensics officers began documenting the phones.

Not grabbing them.

Photographing them where they lay.

Serial numbers.

Condition.

Time.

Chain of custody.

That professionalism unsettled Ian more than disorder would have.

This was not a rogue group improvising.

It was procedure.

Seo-yeon asked:

"Where is my husband?"

Park's expression did not change.

"He is safe."

"Where?"

"I cannot disclose his location."

"Has he been charged?"

"I cannot discuss his status."

"Can he contact counsel?"

"That request is being reviewed."

Min-seok interrupted.

"It has already been reviewed once and denied without written justification."

Park looked at him.

"You will receive documentation."

"When?"

"I don't control that process."

Seo-yeon leaned toward the inspector.

"My husband called me this morning."

Park's eyes changed.

Barely.

Ian saw it.

"What time?" Park asked.

Min-seok answered.

"That is privileged pending clarification of Mr. Kim's custody status."

Park looked toward him.

"The call may be relevant to national security."

"So may your reason for detaining him."

The room went quiet.

Park did not take the bait.

He turned back to Seo-yeon.

"Did your husband mention explosive material?"

"No."

"RDX?"

"No."

"Military-grade compounds?"

"No."

"Foreign contacts?"

"My husband is a structural engineer."

"That is not an answer."

"He has foreign colleagues."

"Which countries?"

Min-seok raised his hand.

"No questioning without agreed scope."

Park paused.

Then nodded.

"We can schedule a formal interview."

One of the forensic officers approached Ian's backpack.

Ian stepped forward.

"That's mine."

The officer stopped.

Park looked at the warrant.

"Devices only."

Ian opened the bag himself.

Laptop.

School tablet.

Battery.

No compass.

It was in his jacket.

The officer bagged the laptop and tablet.

Ian watched.

"Do I get those back?"

"When cleared."

"When?"

"I don't know."

Another official answer.

Ian felt anger rise.

He looked at Park.

"Why did you take my father before the building collapsed?"

The inspector became still.

Seo-yeon said:

"Ian."

He ignored her.

"Why?"

Park looked at Min-seok.

The lawyer did not stop the question.

Finally Park answered.

"Your father was asked to assist an investigation already in progress."

"Into Helios?"

"I cannot answer that."

"Into explosives?"

"I cannot answer that."

"Into terrorism?"

"I cannot answer that."

Ian stepped closer.

"Then what can you answer?"

Park looked at him for a long moment.

"That your father was not taken because the building collapsed."

The room froze.

Seo-yeon's eyes narrowed.

Park realized immediately how the sentence sounded.

He corrected:

"The inquiry involving your father began before the collapse. I cannot tell you whether it was connected to what later occurred."

Ian heard only the first part.

Before.

Confirmed now by the investigator himself.

Park continued.

"Do not infer more than that."

Ian almost laughed.

Everyone kept telling him the same thing.

Don't infer.

Don't conclude.

Don't complete the pattern.

Park collected the seizure inventory.

Then, before leaving, he looked at Seo-yeon.

"Mrs. Yoo, I strongly recommend that you and your son remain reachable."

"Is that an order?"

"No."

"Then don't phrase it like one."

Park nodded slightly.

Perhaps respect.

Perhaps nothing.

The team left.

The door closed.

Ian immediately opened his notebook.

Under KNOWN, he wrote:

Chief Inspector Park: "Your father was not taken because the building collapsed."

Then beneath it:

The inquiry involving Appa began before the collapse.

He underlined the sentence once.

Seo-yeon watched.

"Exact wording."

Ian nodded.

He crossed out his first paraphrase.

Then wrote the quote precisely.

She approved.

Not the conclusion.

The record.

By noon, the raid had expanded across the country.

Television networks showed police entering offices belonging to:

the structural review consortium,

a specialty demolition subcontractor,

two chemical suppliers,

a security contractor,

and a logistics company that had serviced the Helios construction site.

That last one caught Seo-yeon's attention.

She turned up the volume.

"...investigators are examining procurement records associated with controlled blasting compounds and industrial energetic materials. Authorities stress that many such compounds have legitimate construction applications."

Ian looked at her.

"So there could actually be RDX."

"In demolition work? RDX specifically would be unusual for ordinary commercial structural work. But energetic compounds and blasting agents exist in legitimate industrial supply chains."

"Could Appa have known?"

"Not from structural review alone."

The broadcast displayed archival footage of controlled demolition.

Ian watched the building fold inward.

For half a second, it resembled Helios.

Then it didn't.

He looked away.

The more explanations he encountered, the less clean the pattern became.

Accident.

Sabotage.

Controlled material used illegally.

Pre-existing intelligence operation.

Government misconduct.

Coincidence.

None fit everything.

That should have made him cautious.

Instead, uncertainty began to feel like pressure.

He wanted one explanation strong enough to organize the rest.

Seo-yeon noticed him staring at the list.

"Don't."

"What?"

"Pick one because you're tired."

"I'm not."

"You are."

She pointed at the television.

"They are showing you ten minutes of footage and asking your brain to turn it into cause."

Ian closed the notebook.

"Then how long until we know?"

Seo-yeon looked at him.

"I don't know."

He stood.

"I hate that answer."

"So do I."

"No, you don't."

She considered him.

"No."

Then quietly:

"I've learned to live with it."

Ian looked away.

He had not.

At 13:36, Min-seok received the first written confirmation of Ji-man's status.

He read it twice.

Then handed it to Seo-yeon.

The document stated that Kim Ji-man was being held as a material witness and person of investigative interest in connection with a national-security inquiry related to the Helios incident.

No criminal charge.

No terrorism indictment.

No allegation that he possessed explosives.

But his movement remained restricted pending emergency review.

Ian read the page.

"Material witness and person of interest?"

"Deliberately broad," Min-seok said.

"Can they keep him?"

"Temporarily."

"Can we see him?"

"I'm challenging the restriction."

"When?"

"Today."

Ian handed the paper back.

"At least now we know why they took him."

Min-seok shook his head.

"No."

Ian frowned.

"This says Helios."

"This document was issued after Helios collapsed."

Ian understood.

It explained his father's status now.

Not why he had been taken before.

The broken variable remained.

Min-seok closed his laptop.

"We still need the original basis for contact."

"Can you get it?"

"Eventually."

"How long?"

"Days, maybe longer."

Ian stared at him.

His father was somewhere he could not locate.

The official explanation was changing faster than the documents could catch up.

And every answer came with a new time attached to it.

Ian opened his notebook again.

At the top of a fresh page, he wrote:

THE ORDER MATTERS.

Underneath:

Investigation → detention → collapse → terrorism classification

He stared at the arrows.

Then he added a question mark above the first term.

Because he still did not know what the investigation had been.

Seo-yeon looked over his shoulder.

She did not tell him to erase the sequence.

Instead she pointed to the first arrow.

"This one is established."

Then the second.

"This one."

Then the third.

"This one too."

Her finger moved to the implied connection between them.

"This is not."

Ian looked at the gap.

A few centimeters of white paper.

That was where the explanation should have been.

"How long do we leave it blank?"

Seo-yeon answered without hesitation.

"Until something crosses it."

Ian looked down at the notebook.

Outside the conference-room window, aircraft lifted from Gimpo one after another, climbing into a sky that looked perfectly ordinary.

The official investigation was expanding.

His father remained hidden inside it.

And for the first time, Ian understood that a sequence of true events could still conceal the relationship between them.

The facts were accumulating.

The causation was not.

### [Scene 2: The Official Verdict]

At 16:09, the government stopped calling Kim Ji-man a material witness.

The first change appeared on television.

Seo-yeon and Ian were still inside the business hotel near Gimpo when every major network interrupted its regular programming for a joint briefing from the National Police Agency.

The podium carried three emblems.

National Police Agency.

National Forensic Service.

Joint Helios Investigation Team.

No one from the National Intelligence Service stood at the microphones.

That did not mean they were absent from the investigation.

It meant the criminal narrative had reached the point where police were prepared to speak publicly.

Seo-yeon lowered the volume on her phone and turned toward the wall-mounted television.

"Write the time."

Ian opened his notebook.

16:09 — official briefing begins.

Chief Inspector Park Seong-ho was not at the podium.

A deputy commissioner Ian had never seen stepped forward instead.

Behind him, a screen displayed a satellite image of the Helios complex before the collapse.

"The Joint Investigation Team has obtained preliminary evidence indicating that the Helios structural failure may have involved an intentional explosive event within the lower transfer structure."

Cameras clicked.

The official continued.

"Chemical analysis conducted on debris recovered from two restricted-access mechanical spaces has detected residues consistent with cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine, commonly known as RDX."

Ian stopped writing.

RDX.

The word had moved.

Yesterday it had been television speculation.

Now it was inside an official sentence.

Seo-yeon noticed him pause.

"Write what he said."

Ian continued.

The deputy commissioner spoke carefully.

"The presence of explosive residue does not by itself establish the quantity, deployment method, initiating device, or identity of any responsible person. Additional forensic testing is underway."

Seo-yeon said quietly:

"That sentence too."

Ian wrote it.

The official continued.

"Investigators have also recovered digital materials indicating unauthorized access to structural documentation associated with the Helios transfer levels."

A photograph appeared on the screen.

A laptop.

Not his father's.

Then a server rack.

Then a set of printed plans sealed inside transparent evidence bags.

"Several persons with legitimate professional access to the structure are being investigated regarding whether such access was misused."

Ian looked toward Min-seok.

"Several."

The lawyer nodded.

"Listen."

The next slide appeared.

A black rectangle concealed most of a digital message.

Only a few fragments remained visible.

LOAD TRANSFER / LOWER PODIUM

WINDOW CONFIRMED

ACCESS PRIOR TO 14:00

The room seemed to contract.

Ian leaned toward the television.

"What's that?"

Min-seok did not answer.

The deputy commissioner did.

"Encrypted communications recovered during the investigation contain references to structural access windows and load-transfer conditions. Attribution remains under forensic review."

Ian read the line again.

WINDOW CONFIRMED.

Seo-yeon stood.

"That isn't Ji-man."

Nobody had said that it was.

Not yet.

The official continued.

"One individual whose professional role included independent review of the lower transfer structure has been identified as a person of significant investigative interest."

Ian's pen stopped again.

The photograph appeared.

His father.

Not an arrest photograph.

His corporate headshot.

Dark suit.

White shirt.

The faint half-smile Ji-man used whenever someone told him to look natural for a camera.

Ian did not breathe.

Seo-yeon said:

"No."

On television, the deputy commissioner continued speaking in the same neutral tone.

"Mr. Kim Ji-man, forty-eight, a structural engineering consultant associated with the Helios review consortium, was interviewed yesterday as part of a pre-existing national-security inquiry concerning unauthorized access to sensitive infrastructure data."

Ian stared at the screen.

There.

A partial answer.

The inquiry had existed before the collapse.

The official continued.

"Mr. Kim was not under arrest at the time of initial contact."

Min-seok immediately wrote something.

Seo-yeon did not move.

"Following the Helios incident and the recovery of additional evidence, Mr. Kim's status was elevated to person of investigative interest."

Another slide.

A photograph of a small black storage device.

"Investigators recovered encrypted files associated with Mr. Kim's professional accounts containing structural models of the Helios transfer system that differed from approved project documentation."

Ian spoke without looking away.

"Of course they differed."

Seo-yeon turned toward him.

"He was reviewing it."

"That's his job."

Min-seok nodded.

"Yes."

The official had anticipated that objection.

"We emphasize that possession of alternative structural models is not in itself evidence of criminal activity. Structural consultants routinely generate independent calculations."

Ian felt a momentary release.

Then:

"However, investigators are examining whether those files were transmitted to unauthorized external recipients."

A reporter shouted:

"Are you saying Kim Ji-man was involved in the bombing?"

The deputy commissioner raised a hand.

"We are not making that allegation at this time."

Another reporter:

"Was Mr. Kim working with a foreign intelligence service?"

"We have no conclusion to announce regarding foreign involvement."

"Was he detained before the collapse because authorities knew an attack was imminent?"

The room went still.

Ian leaned forward.

The deputy commissioner looked down briefly at his notes.

"The pre-existing inquiry concerned unauthorized handling of infrastructure-related data. I cannot discuss classified intelligence that led to the initial interview."

"So authorities had information before the collapse?"

"I did not say that."

"Did the inquiry concern Helios specifically?"

"I cannot answer that at this stage."

"Was Kim Ji-man suspected of planning sabotage before 14:17 yesterday?"

"I cannot answer that."

Ian looked down at his notebook.

The blank space between detention and collapse remained blank.

The press was asking exactly what he wanted to know.

The government was refusing exactly where the chronology mattered most.

Then a woman entered the conference room behind the podium.

She handed the deputy commissioner a folded sheet of paper.

He read it.

His face changed.

Not much.

Enough.

Seo-yeon saw it first.

"What happened?"

No one in the hotel room answered.

The deputy commissioner whispered to an aide.

The aide nodded.

The cameras continued recording.

Finally the deputy commissioner returned to the microphone.

"There has been a development concerning Mr. Kim."

Ian stood.

Seo-yeon did not.

She seemed unable to.

The official looked directly into the cameras.

"At approximately 15:22 this afternoon, Mr. Kim was found unresponsive at a secure medical evaluation facility in central Seoul, where he had been transferred following his interview."

Ian heard the words.

They did not assemble.

"Emergency medical personnel initiated resuscitation procedures."

The official paused.

"Mr. Kim was pronounced deceased at 15:47."

The room disappeared.

Not visually.

It simply ceased to matter.

Ian looked at his mother.

She was still facing the television.

Her expression had not changed.

That frightened him.

"Umma."

No response.

"Umma."

Seo-yeon reached for the remote control and muted the television.

The deputy commissioner continued speaking silently.

His mouth moved.

Cameras flashed.

Ian could hear only the hotel ventilation system.

Min-seok stood slowly.

"I'll confirm it."

Seo-yeon said:

"No."

The lawyer stopped.

She looked at him.

"Confirm it now."

He took out his phone.

Confirmation took seven minutes.

It felt longer than the previous two days.

Min-seok made three calls.

The first went unanswered.

The second transferred him twice.

The third ended with him walking to the far side of the conference room.

Ian watched his face.

That was enough.

Min-seok returned.

"It's confirmed."

Seo-yeon closed her eyes.

Ian remained standing.

"How?"

Min-seok looked toward him.

"We don't know yet."

Ian hated him for the answer.

"How did he die?"

"Police are saying apparent fall trauma."

"Fall from where?"

"A service terrace."

"What floor?"

"I don't know."

"Was he alone?"

"I don't know."

"Why was he on a terrace?"

"I don't know."

Ian kicked the chair away from him.

It struck the wall.

Seo-yeon opened her eyes.

"Ian."

"He was in custody."

"Yes."

"They said he was safe."

"I know."

"They wouldn't tell us where."

"I know."

"They wouldn't let the lawyer see him."

"I know."

"And now he's dead."

Seo-yeon stood.

Her voice did not rise.

"I know."

The two words stopped him.

For the first time, her control cracked.

Not into crying.

Into anger.

"You do not have to explain my husband's death to me."

Ian looked away.

Seo-yeon took one breath.

Then another.

She reached for her notebook.

"Time."

Ian stared at her.

"What?"

"Time of death notification."

"Umma—"

"Write it."

Her hand was shaking.

She pressed it flat against the table.

"Write it while we know it."

Ian picked up his pen.

16:16 — counsel independently confirms Ji-man deceased.

Then:

Police state: found unresponsive approx. 15:22. Pronounced dead 15:47.

His handwriting deteriorated halfway through the second line.

He stopped.

Seo-yeon took the notebook from him and finished it herself.

The police briefing resumed twenty-three minutes later.

This time Min-seok insisted they watch.

Ian did not want to.

Seo-yeon did.

That decided it.

The deputy commissioner returned to the podium.

"The circumstances of Mr. Kim's death are being investigated separately by the Seoul Metropolitan Police and National Forensic Service."

A reporter shouted:

"Was it suicide?"

"The preliminary physical evidence is consistent with a fall from height. We will not make a final determination until forensic examination is complete."

"Was he under guard?"

"Mr. Kim was under controlled movement restrictions."

"How did he reach an exterior terrace?"

"That is under investigation."

"Was there CCTV?"

"Yes."

"Will it be released?"

"Not at this time."

Another reporter:

"Was there a note?"

The deputy commissioner paused.

"A written document was recovered among Mr. Kim's personal effects."

Ian looked at his mother.

Her face went blank.

"What document?" a reporter asked.

"We are analyzing it."

"Suicide note?"

"We are not characterizing it until authentication is complete."

The questions multiplied.

The official eventually raised his voice.

"I will repeat: no final conclusion regarding manner of death has been reached."

That was the careful sentence.

The headlines were not careful.

Within ten minutes:

HELIOS PERSON OF INTEREST DEAD IN APPARENT SUICIDE

Then:

STRUCTURAL ENGINEER LINKED TO HELIOS PROBE DIES AFTER FALL

Then:

SUICIDE NOTE FOUND IN HELIOS SABOTAGE INVESTIGATION

The official language had not yet said suicide.

The public language already had.

Ian watched the transformation happen in real time.

Possibility became headline.

Headline became repetition.

Repetition became memory.

They were permitted to see Ji-man's body at 21:40.

Not at the secure facility.

At the National Forensic Service mortuary.

Min-seok accompanied them.

A police liaison met them at the entrance.

She was younger than Ian expected.

Detective Lee Hye-jin.

Plain clothes.

No visible weapon.

She bowed slightly to Seo-yeon.

"I'm sorry for your loss."

Seo-yeon did not respond.

Lee did not appear offended.

She led them through a corridor that smelled of disinfectant and cold air.

Ian had expected something dramatic.

There was only bureaucracy.

Forms.

Identification.

A plastic visitor card.

A signature acknowledging that the body remained subject to forensic examination.

A request not to touch certain areas.

The ordinary administration of death.

Before they entered the viewing room, Detective Lee stopped them.

"There is visible trauma."

Seo-yeon looked at her.

"His face?"

"Mostly intact."

"Mostly?"

"He sustained impact injuries. We have cleaned what we can without disturbing evidence."

Ian felt his stomach tighten.

Seo-yeon asked:

"Can my son wait outside?"

Ian answered before the detective could.

"No."

His mother looked at him.

He held her gaze.

She nodded.

The door opened.

Ji-man lay beneath a white sheet.

For several seconds, Ian did not recognize him.

Not because of the injuries.

Because his father was still.

Ji-man had always moved.

A pencil between fingers.

A cup in one hand.

A foot tapping beneath the table when he read calculations.

His stillness was the most unnatural thing in the room.

Seo-yeon walked to the table.

She touched his hair.

The detective did not stop her.

Ian remained near the door.

There was bruising near one temple.

A cut above the eyebrow.

One side of the neck showed dark discoloration.

His father's hands were visible.

Ian stared at them.

The fingers looked ordinary.

That felt offensive.

Those hands had held the compass two nights ago.

They should have looked different now.

Marked.

Changed.

Something.

They did not.

Seo-yeon whispered:

"Ji-man."

No response.

Of course.

Ian moved closer.

He did not cry.

He wanted to.

Nothing happened.

He looked at the body and waited for grief to become a physical event.

It did not.

Instead he noticed details.

A small abrasion across the right knuckle.

Dry skin near the thumb.

A faint adhesive mark on the forearm where a medical line had been attached.

The clean edge where his father's watch should have been.

Ian hated himself for seeing these things.

"Where's his watch?"

Detective Lee looked at him.

"Personal effects are being held."

"His phone?"

"Held."

"Wallet?"

"Held."

"Compass?"

Seo-yeon turned.

Ian realized what he had said.

His father had not been carrying the compass.

It was in Ian's pocket.

He touched it through the fabric.

Detective Lee continued.

"Personal effects will be released after the evidence review."

Seo-yeon looked down at her husband's body.

"Was he handcuffed?"

The detective paused.

"Not at the time he was found."

"Before?"

"During some transfers, yes."

"Was he restrained when he reached the terrace?"

"No."

"Who opened the door?"

"We are reviewing access logs."

"Was anyone with him?"

"The nearest officer was inside the corridor."

"How far?"

"I don't have the finalized reconstruction."

Seo-yeon looked at her.

"Then don't give me preliminary words that sound final."

Detective Lee absorbed that.

"Understood."

Ian studied her.

"Did he jump?"

Lee answered carefully.

"We don't know."

"Did he fall?"

"We know he fell."

"From how high?"

"Approximately eleven stories."

Ian's eyes moved toward his mother.

Something changed in Seo-yeon's face.

Not surprise.

Memory.

"Eleven."

Lee nodded.

Seo-yeon looked back at Ji-man.

"He couldn't stand on our apartment balcony."

The detective said nothing.

Ian looked at her.

His mother continued.

"Sixth floor."

She touched Ji-man's hair again.

"He wouldn't go near the railing."

Ian remembered.

Family trips.

Observation decks avoided.

Glass elevators hated.

His father refusing to change a light bulb near an open stairwell and claiming the problem was "bad access geometry."

Acrophobia.

The word entered Ian's mind with the force of proof.

"He wouldn't jump."

Detective Lee looked at him.

Ian stepped closer.

"He was afraid of heights."

Seo-yeon said:

"Ian."

"No. He was."

"I know."

"He wouldn't do that."

Detective Lee spoke quietly.

"Fear of heights is relevant background."

Ian turned on her.

"Relevant?"

"It is not conclusive."

"What does that mean?"

"It means people sometimes act contrary to long-standing fears under acute distress."

"My father wasn't suicidal."

"I did not say he was."

"The news did."

"I am not the news."

Ian stared at her.

Lee continued.

"If you want the investigation to be accurate, give us facts. Medical history. Behavioral history. Anything he said. But don't ask me to convert one fact into a conclusion before the rest exists."

It was almost exactly what his mother kept saying.

That made him angrier.

Seo-yeon placed one hand on Ian's arm.

"She is right."

He turned.

"Umma."

"She is right about that."

"He was afraid."

"I know."

"You know what he was like."

"I do."

"Then why are you—"

"Because knowing him is not the same as knowing how he died."

The sentence broke something.

Ian stepped away from the table.

He could not look at either of them.

The autopsy began the following morning.

Seo-yeon formally requested an independent observer.

Min-seok found one: Professor Choi Min-jun, a forensic pathologist from a university hospital unaffiliated with the Helios investigation.

Police objected.

Min-seok insisted.

They compromised.

Choi would not participate directly but would receive photographs, imaging, and selected findings for independent review after the statutory examination.

Ian was not allowed into any part of the process.

He sat in a waiting room with a vending machine that sold canned coffee and bottled water.

On the wall, a television displayed a muted financial channel.

Helios Group shares had been suspended.

Construction companies tied to the project fell across the market.

Insurance analysts discussed aggregate liability.

Five hundred and twelve confirmed dead.

One hundred and forty-seven missing.

The numbers climbed as if the disaster were still happening.

At 10:14, an alert appeared on Ian's phone.

POLICE AUTHENTICATE DOCUMENT RECOVERED FROM KIM JI-MAN

He opened it.

The article quoted unnamed investigative sources.

A handwritten page had been found inside Ji-man's personal notebook.

The source claimed it contained:

"I made a mistake that cannot be repaired."

Ian read the sentence.

Again.

Then again.

His hands went cold.

Seo-yeon returned from speaking with Min-seok.

She saw his face.

"What?"

Ian showed her.

She read the article.

"No."

"Could he have written it?"

"Those words?"

"Yes."

"I don't know."

"Would he?"

She sat beside him.

"Your father wrote notes to himself constantly."

"What kind?"

"Work. Lists. Arguments. Things he thought he'd calculated wrong."

Ian remembered the notebooks being seized.

"Maybe it wasn't a suicide note."

"Maybe."

"They're calling it one."

"Some sources are."

"Police?"

"Not officially."

Ian scrolled.

Another outlet had already removed the conditional language.

KIM JI-MAN LEFT NOTE ADMITTING "IRREPARABLE MISTAKE" BEFORE SUICIDE

Ian showed her.

"See?"

Seo-yeon stared at the headline.

Her face became very still.

Then she took out her notebook.

"What are you doing?"

"Writing the exact wording from the first report."

"Why?"

"Because by tonight no one will remember which version came first."

Ian watched her copy the sentence.

Then:

Context unknown. Full page not released.

She underlined it.

"Never quote a fragment as if it were the whole document."

Ian looked again at the article.

The sentence felt less solid now.

Not false.

Unlocated.

A piece torn from a larger structure.

At 12:32, Min-seok obtained a copy of the handwritten page.

Not the original.

A scanned image.

They viewed it on his laptop.

Ji-man's handwriting was unmistakable.

Small.

Compressed.

Numbers in the margin.

A sketch of what appeared to be the Helios lower transfer structure.

The quoted sentence was there.

But so were the words before it.

Ian read aloud.

"I made a mistake that cannot be repaired."

He stopped.

Below it:

I assumed the boundary stiffness remained within the design envelope after the revision. It did not.

Then:

That error changes the expected failure sequence.

And below that:

But it still does not explain the sensor timing.

Ian stared.

Seo-yeon closed her eyes.

Min-seok leaned closer to the screen.

"This isn't a suicide note."

Ian looked at him.

"It doesn't look like one."

"It's an engineering note."

"Probably."

"Probably?"

Min-seok pointed at the page.

"We still don't know when he wrote it."

Ian checked the metadata printed at the bottom.

The paper had been photographed during evidence processing after Ji-man's death.

No creation time.

No page sequence.

No original notebook context.

Seo-yeon said:

"They took one sentence."

"Someone leaked one sentence," Min-seok corrected.

"From an engineering calculation."

"Yes."

"And television turned it into a confession."

"Yes."

Ian felt the pressure behind his eyes.

For the first time, one item moved cleanly in his notebook.

He opened to KNOWN.

He wrote:

The quoted "irreparable mistake" sentence comes from an engineering note discussing a structural modeling assumption.

Then:

Public reporting omitted the surrounding text.

He looked at his mother.

"This is lying."

Seo-yeon shook her head.

"Be precise."

"They made it sound like he confessed."

"Somebody leaked a fragment. Reporters interpreted it."

"That's still lying."

"Maybe."

"How can you say maybe?"

"Because we don't know who leaked it, what they intended, or whether some reporter saw only the fragment."

Ian stared at her.

"But the result is the same."

"No."

She closed the laptop halfway.

"Intent and result are different variables."

He hated that too.

The preliminary forensic findings arrived after dark.

Cause of death:

Multiple traumatic injuries resulting from fall from height.

Manner of death:

Undetermined pending investigation.

No lethal drug concentration.

No evidence of gunshot or stab injury.

Minor bruising on wrists consistent with prior restraint.

No clear defensive injury sufficient to establish physical struggle.

No result Ian could point to and say murder.

No result police could honestly point to and say suicide.

The body answered one question.

The fall killed him.

It did not answer why he fell.

Seo-yeon read the report at the hotel table.

Ian stood beside her.

"Undetermined."

"Yes."

"So the headlines are wrong."

"The headlines are ahead of the evidence."

"That's a polite way of saying wrong."

She looked up at him.

"For now, yes."

He took the report.

"If he was pushed, wouldn't there be injuries?"

"Maybe."

"If he fought."

"Maybe."

"And if he didn't?"

"Then maybe not."

Ian slammed the document onto the table.

"Everything is maybe."

Seo-yeon let him.

"Yes."

"How do you live like this?"

She did not answer immediately.

Finally:

"By not pretending the uncertainty disappeared because I hate it."

Ian turned away.

That sentence followed him across the room.

The police formally released their preliminary reconstruction the next morning.

Ji-man had been transferred to a secure medical evaluation center after reporting dizziness and chest discomfort during questioning.

Medical examination found no acute cardiac event.

At approximately 15:17, he requested permission to use the restroom.

According to the official report, while returning under escort he paused near a staff corridor.

A security door leading to an exterior maintenance terrace had been temporarily unlocked because contractors had serviced ventilation equipment earlier that day.

At 15:20, Ji-man entered the corridor.

The escorting officer initially believed he had turned toward the restroom.

Eleven seconds later, the officer discovered the open terrace door.

At 15:22, Ji-man was found on a lower service roof.

CCTV coverage existed in the main corridor.

The interior staff corridor had no camera.

The terrace had no camera.

The event itself was not recorded.

Ian read the sequence twice.

"Eleven seconds."

Seo-yeon nodded.

"He disappeared from the camera for eleven seconds?"

"The released summary says the escort lost direct visual contact for approximately that long."

"And that's enough?"

"For what?"

"To climb over a barrier?"

"We don't know what the barrier looked like."

Min-seok brought up facility photographs released with the report.

A service terrace.

Concrete floor.

Mechanical ducting.

Metal safety barrier approximately chest height.

Ian stared at it.

His father had been afraid to stand against a glass balcony railing six floors up.

This was eleven.

"He wouldn't."

Seo-yeon touched the screen.

"Write it under background."

Ian looked at her.

"Not known?"

"Known: your father had longstanding fear of exposed heights."

"And conclusion?"

"Unknown."

Ian did not write.

His mother took the notebook and wrote it herself.

KNOWN: Ji-man had longstanding severe discomfort/fear around exposed heights.

Then:

INFERENCE: voluntary jump appears inconsistent with known behavior.

Below:

LIMIT: behavior under acute distress cannot be reconstructed from this fact alone.

Ian stared at the three lines.

The structure of the page felt cruel.

It allowed nothing to become absolute.

The official Helios narrative hardened over the following forty-eight hours.

Forensic teams reported RDX residue at multiple locations near the lower transfer zone.

Investigators identified unauthorized late-night access to service corridors in the week before the collapse.

Several contractors were detained.

One subcontractor admitted falsifying access-control records.

A procurement intermediary had purchased restricted electronic detonator components under a false company name.

These were real developments.
