"Because you keep talking about it like it betrayed you."

Ian frowned.

"It removed control authority during the peak event."

"It refused to become a fire."

"Both can be true."

"Yes."

Aris nodded.

"Now you're talking like an engineer."

Ian looked at the exposed conductor.

"So what's the redesign?"

"Too early."

"More cooling."

"Maybe."

"Lower-loss conductor."

"Maybe."

"More reserve."

"Probably."

"Independent local thermal model."

"Yes."

"Second joint temperature reference."

"Probably."

"Faster current redistribution."

Aris shook his head.

"Careful."

"Why?"

"Fast isn't always better."

"Less hotspot energy."

"More voltage."

"Then insulation."

"More mass."

"Then—"

Aris raised a hand.

"There."

"What?"

"You've started building the infinite machine again."

Ian stopped.

Aris pointed at Node Four.

"This is what control costs."

Ian looked.

"Stored energy."

"That."

"Cryogenics."

"That."

"Mass."

"That."

"Redundancy."

"That."

"Complexity."

"That."

"Time."

Aris nodded.

"Mostly time."

Ian looked toward the other nodes.

"Vance says someone will miniaturize it."

"Of course."

"You think it's possible?"

"Everything can get smaller."

"Not everything."

"Fine. Most expensive things can get smaller if you spend enough money making the first version enormous."

"That's not physics."

"It's history."

Ian almost smiled.

Aris removed his gloves.

"The problem isn't making one coil smaller."

"No."

"It's power density."

"Yes."

"Heat."

"Yes."

"Field shape."

"Yes."

"Margin."

"Yes."

"Timing."

"Yes."

"Control hardware."

"Yes."

"Structure."

"Yes."

"Radiation if you put it in space."

"Yes."

"Then why are you asking whether it fits in a truck?"

"Vance asked."

Aris laughed.

"Of course."

They stood in silence.

Then Aris said:

"What did they decide upstairs?"

"No single operator."

"Good."

"Preauthorized classes."

"Good."

"Restrictions on high-amplitude actuator details."

Aris looked at him.

"Your idea?"

"Partly."

He considered.

"Good."

Ian looked.

"You don't care about openness?"

"I care whether some idiot builds a coil from a conference slide."

"Replication matters."

"Yes."

"Then—"

"Give competent people enough to replicate the physics."

He pointed toward Node Four.

"Not enough to reproduce our mistakes at ten times the current."

Ian nodded.

Fair.

Aris turned back toward the node.

Ian said:

"One question."

"No."

"You don't know what it is."

"Still no."

"If yesterday had required damaging Four to keep the boundary?"

Aris stopped.

"What do you mean?"

"If local protection had withdrawn, but an override could have preserved the field long enough to prevent the boundary from collapsing."

"No."

"You don't know the scenario."

"I know the answer."

"If people were inside?"

"No."

"If hundreds?"

"No."

"Aris."

He turned.

"Because you are hiding the actual question."

Ian stared.

"What is it?"

"How much machine are you willing to destroy to save people?"

"Yes."

"No."

"Then what?"

"Whether destroying the machine actually saves them."

Ian said nothing.

Aris continued.

"If you know the override works and the coil dies afterward, fine."

"Fine?"

"Expensive."

"And if uncertain?"

"Then a dead coil plus dead people is not courage."

He looked back at Four.

"The cost of control includes knowing when you do not have it."

Ian left.

At 11:20, he found Sterling in the original NGC control corridor.

Not the new G-DCL room.

The old corridor.

Near the evidence cabinet containing the Sector Four FPGA.

Sterling was looking through the glass.

Ian stopped beside him.

"What are you doing?"

"Remembering."

"I didn't know you did that."

"Rarely."

The FPGA remained unchanged.

A small black chassis.

One local machine.

One old solver.

The device that had saved the NGC when the central system became unreliable.

Ian said:

"They should remove it."

Sterling looked at him.

"Why?"

"It's becoming symbolic."

"Of what?"

"Depends who looks."

"Then leave it."

Ian frowned.

"That's an argument for museums."

"Occasionally civilization benefits from remembering that history was once uncertain."

Ian leaned against the wall.

"They want activation authority."

"I know."

"National versions."

"I know."

"Defense applications."

"I know."

"Restrictions."

"I know."

Ian looked at him.

"You knew this would happen."

"Of course."

"Then why approve the public finding?"

Sterling turned.

"Because it was true."

"Even if the result is dangerous?"

"Especially then."

Ian frowned.

"That makes no sense."

"No. It prevents you from believing danger changes measurement."

Sterling looked through the cabinet again.

"What did your father tell you?"

Ian stiffened.

"About what?"

"Structures."

Ian remembered.

Nothing built by people is perfect. The question is whether the imperfection is known, bounded, and survivable.

He did not speak.

Sterling apparently knew anyway.

"He taught you something useful."

"Yes."

"And you turned it into something else."

Ian looked at him.

"What?"

"A promise."

Silence.

"That if the variables were known, the world could be made safe from interpretation."

"That's not what I—"

Sterling looked at him.

Ian stopped.

Fine.

Maybe it was.

Sterling continued.

"Yesterday was not the conclusion you wanted."

"No."

"You did not discover the mechanism."

"No."

"You did not prove your ontology."

"No."

"You did not restore the entire region to baseline."

"No."

"You did not predict the first transition correctly."

Ian looked away.

"No."

"And yet?"

"We changed the response."

"Yes."

Sterling nodded.

"You finally have a result strong enough that you no longer need to exaggerate it."

Ian looked at him.

"That's supposed to be comforting?"

"It should be."

It was.

A little.

Ian said:

"And now everyone wants the machine."

"Yes."

"We can't let every government build one independently."

"Why?"

Ian stared.

"Because some will use it badly."

"Probably."

"Then we need control."

Sterling's expression changed almost imperceptibly.

"There."

Ian frowned.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Say it."

Sterling looked directly at him.

"You have become more comfortable with uncertainty."

"Yes."

"And less comfortable with anyone else having authority over it."

Ian said nothing.

"This is different."

"Of course."

"Science requires openness."

"Yes."

"Capability requires governance."

"Yes."

"Then where is the problem?"

Sterling looked toward the old FPGA.

"The problem is not the sentence."

"What sentence?"

"We need control."

Ian waited.

"The problem is who you mean by we."

The corridor seemed quieter.

Ian looked at Sterling.

"The international program."

"Perhaps."

"Independent science board."

"Perhaps."

"Operators."

"Perhaps."

Sterling waited.

Ian understood the trap.

"And me."

Sterling did not answer.

That was worse.

Ian pushed away from the wall.

"I wrote the model."

"Yes."

"I understand the control system better than anyone."

"Possibly."

"Don't."

"Then don't give me claims you don't want qualified."

Ian glared.

Sterling continued.

"You understand one part of it exceptionally well."

"Enough to know what can go wrong."

"No."

Ian stopped.

Sterling pointed down the corridor.

"Sarah knows things you don't."

"Yes."

"Aris."

"Yes."

"Mori."

"Yes."

"Park."

"Yes."

"The pilots who flew Flight 702."

"That's different."

"Exactly."

Sterling looked at him.

"There is no one vantage point from which all consequences of this technology become visible."

Ian said:

"So diffuse responsibility until no one can act?"

"No."

"That's what committees do."

"Bad ones."

"Then what?"

Sterling thought.

"Do what the machine did."

Ian stared.

"What?"

"Share the objective."

"That's not governance."

"Maintain local authority."

"People aren't nodes."

"Correct."

"Then stop making hardware analogies."

Sterling nodded.

"Good."

Ian almost swore.

Sterling continued.

"But the design principle remains useful."

"Which?"

"No one actor should be able to turn a local error into the whole system."

Ian looked toward the old FPGA.

"That requires vetoes."

"Yes."

"Which create delay."

"Yes."

"Which can kill people."

"Yes."

"And central authority can act faster."

"Yes."

"And misuse power faster."

"Yes."

Ian stared.

Sterling had become infuriatingly comfortable with both sides being true.

Maybe that was maturity.

Maybe exhaustion.

Ian said:

"At some point, someone has to decide."

"Yes."

"Then responsibility cannot be distributed forever."

"No."

"Someone owns the decision."

"Yes."

"Who?"

Sterling looked at him.

"That is not a physics problem."

Ian disliked the answer.

Because it was true.

At 13:07, Sarah sent him a message.

Come upstairs.

No explanation.

He went.

The international steering group had received a new request.

Not from one country.

From six.

A joint proposal for:

PORTABLE DISTRIBUTED RESPONSE MODULE FEASIBILITY STUDY

Ian read it.

"Portable."

Sarah nodded.

"They moved quickly."

"How portable?"

"No specification."

"Then meaningless."

"Read the next page."

He did.

Candidate objectives:

vehicle-scale node architecture.

modular cryogenic system.

compact high-field actuators.

local optical timing.

self-contained power.

rapid deployment.

urban infrastructure protection.

airfield protection.

mobile scientific response.

The words were benign.

Mostly.

Then:

localized directional-response control

Ian stopped.

"There."

Sarah nodded.

"Yes."

"Who added it?"

"Unknown."

"Remove it."

"We don't own the proposal."

"Then reject it."

"We don't own the steering group either."

Ian looked at her.

"So why show me?"

"Because they want our technical assessment."

Vance entered.

Of course.

Ian looked at him.

"You knew."

"I helped write the manufacturing feasibility section."

"You included directional response."

"No."

"Who did?"

"Not my part."

"Convenient."

Vance stared.

"You think I'm trying to build a gravity weapon in a truck?"

"No."

"Good."

Ian hesitated.

Vance noticed.

"That's insulting."

"You're Vance."

"Also true."

Sarah said:

"Technical assessment."

Ian looked at the request again.

Portable.

The G-DCL required a collider-class site.

That limitation was currently their best safety feature.

Not intentionally.

But effectively.

Miniaturization would change everything.

A system small enough to deploy quickly could protect.

A system small enough to deploy quickly could also be placed where someone else did not want it.

A boundary could become movable.

Private.

Military.

Commercial.

A property line written into local physics.

Ian said:

"Reject full feasibility."

Vance raised an eyebrow.

"Why?"

"We don't know enough."

"That's what feasibility studies are for."

"Some questions should wait."

Vance looked at Sarah.

"Who is this?"

She did not smile.

Ian continued.

"Approve component miniaturization."

"Which components?"

"Power electronics."

"Yes."

"Metrology."

"Yes."

"Cryogenics."

"Yes."

"Conductor."

"Yes."

"Local control hardware."

"Yes."

"Integrated field module?"

"No."

Vance leaned back.

"You want all the pieces smaller but not assembled."

"For now."

"How long does for now last?"

"Until governance catches up."

Vance laughed once.

Not mocking.

Almost sad.

"Governance does not catch technology."

Sarah said:

"It can shape deployment."

"Sometimes."

"That's enough."

Vance looked at Ian.

"You know someone else will integrate it."

Ian said:

"Then we keep critical control details restricted."

"Someone else will derive them."

"Later."

"Maybe."

"Time matters."

Vance nodded.

"Yes."

The word carried his entire worldview.

He owned waiting.

Ian remembered.

Sarah looked at Ian.

"You are proposing delay."

"Yes."

"You hate delay."

"Not when delay is protective."

She considered him.

"That's new."

"Don't."

Vance brought up a second map.

Not factories this time.

Research clusters.

National laboratories.

universities.

aerospace firms.

superconducting magnet programs.

precision timing groups.

High-field fusion programs.

space agencies.

The expertise needed to reconstruct parts of G-DCL already existed across the world.

No one had all of it.

Yet.

Vance said:

"You are not deciding whether miniaturization happens."

Ian looked.

"You are deciding whether the international program is first."

That was different.

And worse.

"If we don't do it," Vance continued, "someone with weaker safety architecture may."

"That's an argument everyone uses to justify going faster."

"Because sometimes it's true."

"And sometimes it becomes self-fulfilling."

"Also true."

Vance looked at the map.

"You cannot uninvent the result."

"No."

"You can make the safest implementation the easiest one to copy."

Sarah said:

"Open safety architecture."

"Exactly."

"Restrict dangerous scaling."

"Yes."

"Standardize local veto."

"Yes."

"Independent clocks."

"Yes."

"Fail silent."

"Yes."

Ian looked between them.

"You two agreeing is disturbing."

Sarah zoomed into the proposal.

"What if we define a modular program with no high-amplitude directional mode?"

Ian thought.

"Hardware may still support it."

"Software limits."

"Can be removed."

"Physical asymmetry."

Vance looked interested.

"Design hardware that is good at bounded cancellation and bad at directed amplification."

Ian frowned.

"Maybe."

Now it was an engineering problem.

Could actuator geometry make certain harmful modes expensive?

Could local controllers enforce symmetric limits?

Could hardware topology restrict gradients?

Could a protection device embody a bias toward stabilization?

Not absolute.

Nothing prevented redesign.

But default architecture mattered.

Ian said:

"Control basis could be constrained."

Sarah nodded.

"Low-order cancellation modes only."

"Limited orientation authority."

"Gradient caps physically enforced."

"Main bias unable to support rapid directional switching."

Vance said:

"Which makes protection slower."

"Yes."

"Less commercially attractive."

"Good."

Vance looked offended.

"That is not a design criterion."

"It is now."

The conversation continued for two hours.

By the end, they approved no portable system.

Only a study of components and safety-constrained architectures.

No integrated vehicle.

No deployment prototype.

No human testing.

No directional amplification experiments above existing low-level commissioning limits.

No relaxation of local veto.

No remote central override.

The program would study how to make the machine smaller without making its worst behaviors easier.

Ian knew that sentence contained optimism.

Maybe arrogance.

Still.

It was better than pretending miniaturization would wait for permission.

At 17:26, everyone left.

Ian did not.

Sarah was packing.

He said:

"Do you think we can control who builds it?"

She looked at him.

"No."

The answer surprised him.

"Then what are we doing?"

"Controlling what we build."

"That's not enough."

"No."

"Then?"

"Making evidence available."

"Standards."

"Safety."

"Independent replication."

"Institutions."

"None of that stops someone."

"No."

Ian looked away.

She waited.

He said:

"I don't like that."

"I know."

"What if someone uses it to make a boundary around a military site?"

"We deal with that."

"What if they exclude observation?"

"We deal with that."

"What if they build a field that rotates local support instead of stabilizing it?"

"We deal with that."

"What if they're first?"

Sarah stopped packing.

"Ian."

"What?"

"You are asking the same question with different nouns."

He stared.

"What question?"

"How do I make sure nothing important happens outside my control?"

The room became quiet.

He said:

"That's not fair."

"Probably."

"This is dangerous."

"Yes."

"I'm talking about responsibility."

"Yes."

"Not certainty."

"Maybe."

Ian looked at her.

She continued.

"You used to want enough knowledge that no one could rewrite the answer."

He said nothing.

"Now you want enough control that no one can misuse the answer."

"That's different."

"Yes."

"Entirely."

"No."

He frowned.

Sarah zipped the case.

"The shape is familiar."

Ian stood.

"Then what do you suggest?"

"Nothing grand."

"Useful."

"Build slowly where slowness buys safety."

"Fast where delay only creates vulnerability."

"Keep independent observers."

"Make nodes refuse us."

"Make institutions refuse us."

"Publish failures."

"Keep the things we are tempted to hide because they're embarrassing."

She looked at him.

"And don't confuse being the person who understands the model with being the person who should own the boundary."

Ian did not answer.

Sarah left.

He remained.

At 18:12, the building was mostly empty.

Ian opened his notebook.

The pages from the last days spread backward.

The boundary held.

We changed it.

Who chooses the target state?

Who chooses the boundary?

Who is allowed inside it?

He turned to a clean page.

At the top:

THE COST OF CONTROL

He began with engineering.

Node count.

Power.

Cryogenics.

thermal margin.

conductor.

timing.

measurement.

hardware redundancy.

industrial capacity.

Then stopped.

Those were costs.

Not the cost.

He crossed out the heading.

Wrote:

CONTROL REQUIRES EXCLUSION

He stared.

Too strong.

Crossed it out.

CONTROL REQUIRES A DEFINITION OF ACCEPTABLE STATES.

Better.

Then:

A protection system must decide what it preserves.

A distributed system must decide what each node may refuse.

An institution must decide who may command, veto, observe, and audit.

He paused.

Then:

A boundary is not only geometry. It is a decision.

That sentence remained.

He thought of Seoul.

Inside the building, floor and down had separated.

The structure survived because neighboring pieces of matter did not all experience the same relationship in the same way.

He thought of Flight 702.

The aircraft carried its history.

Not the Atlantic.

He thought of the Pacific.

Water had risen because the familiar relationship between pressure, propagation, and support had come apart.

Every event had separated things civilization assumed belonged together.

Now G-DCL had done something similar intentionally.

Inside.

Outside.

Protected.

Unprotected.

Target.

Residual.

Safe.

Unsafe.

Those were not properties waiting in nature.

Not all of them.

Some were choices.

At 18:40, Vance returned.

Ian looked up.

"Why are you still here?"

"I could ask you."

"You don't work here."

"Neither do you, technically."

Ian closed the notebook.

Vance sat opposite him.

No laptop.

Again.

That was becoming more worrying than the laptop.

"What?"

Vance asked:

"Do you know why investors like control?"

Ian stared.

"This is going somewhere unpleasant."

"Because uncertainty is expensive."

"Obviously."

"No."

Vance leaned back.

"Volatility is manageable."

"Insurance."

"Hedges."

"Options."

"Redundancy."

"Exactly."

He looked toward the underground levels.

"Unowned uncertainty is what markets hate."

Ian frowned.

"Unowned."

"If no one knows who can act, everyone prices the worst case."

"And?"

"Once someone owns the response, risk becomes a contract."

Ian stared.

"You're talking about selling protection."

"Eventually."

"No."

"Why?"

"Because this isn't insurance."

"Not yet."

"People don't buy access to gravity."

Vance smiled slightly.

"They buy access to everything else."

Ian looked away.

"Don't turn this into a market."

"You think governments won't?"

"That's different."

"Why?"

"Public safety."

"Funding."

"Control."

"Sovereignty."

Vance nodded.

"Markets with flags."

Ian glared.

Vance continued.

"Someone will eventually ask whether one city gets a boundary before another."

"No."

"Of course."

"Not if the program is international."

"Especially then."

"Why?"

"Scarcity."

The answer was immediate.

Vance counted.

"How many Geneva-class systems can you build in five years?"

"Unknown."

"Not many."

"No."

"How many cities?"

Ian said nothing.

"Airports?"

Nothing.

"Data centers?"

Nothing.

"Military facilities?"

Nothing.

"Power grids?"

Nothing.

Vance lowered his hand.

"Every boundary you build somewhere is a boundary you did not build somewhere else."

Ian looked at him.

"That's allocation."

"Yes."

"Not physics."

"No."

"The technology could become cheaper."

"Eventually."

"Smaller."

"Probably."

"Then scarcity falls."

"Maybe."

Vance looked toward the door.

"But the first generation will be scarce."

A pause.

"And first-generation scarcity creates owners."

Ian said:

"No private ownership."

Vance raised an eyebrow.

"Of G-DCL?"

"Of high-amplitude systems."

"Governments only?"

"International authority."

"Which governments own."

"Not own."

"Vote."

"Govern."

"Allocate."

"Yes."

Vance looked at him.

"Words."

Ian felt irritation rising.

"What do you want?"

"Nothing."

"That's a lie."

"I want you to understand the problem before you try to solve it with access control."

Ian stared.

Vance continued.

"If you lock the technology down, the people with the strongest states get it first."

"If you open it, anyone can weaponize it."

"Yes."

"If we commercialize it, wealth determines access."

"Yes."

"If international organizations allocate it, politics determines access."

"Yes."

"Then what solution do you have?"

Vance smiled without humor.

"None."

Ian looked at him.

"Useful."

"That's why it's your next problem."

Ian leaned back.

"I solve physical systems."

"No."

Vance shook his head.

"You used to."

"What does that mean?"

"Yesterday you created scarcity around a physical law."

"We didn't create the law."

"You created access to altering its effect."

"Locally."

"Enough."

Vance leaned forward.

"Once a physical phenomenon has an actuator, it has a politics."

Ian said nothing.

Vance stood.

At the door he stopped.

"One more thing."

"What?"

"You keep asking how to prevent someone else from controlling it."

"Yes."

"Be careful."

"Why?"

"That's how people decide they're the exception."

Then he left.

Ian sat alone.

He disliked Vance most when Vance was useful.

At 20:03, Ian descended one last time to the G-DCL overlook.

Night mode.

Node Four dark.

Eleven nodes standby.

The central test volume empty.

Pendulum vertical.

Tungsten heavy.

Optical channels close to baseline.

No anomaly.

No boundary.

The machine had returned to being absurdly large infrastructure around a room where nothing unusual was happening.

He looked at the twelve node positions.

One missing from readiness.

The symmetry broken.

Still a system.

He thought of the first Geneva event.

One local FPGA acting when the center failed.

Then Denver.

One room.

One mass.

Gravity nearly absent.

Inertia remaining.

Then twelve nodes.

Then the world.

The technology had grown in scale because the problem had grown in scale.

Now the next breakthrough would probably reverse that.

Smaller.

Portable.

Cheaper.

Harder to supervise.

The machine's physical cost would fall.

Its political cost would rise.

Sterling's words returned.

The problem is who you mean by we.

Ian did not like questions without a mathematical resolution.

This one might never have one.

He opened the notebook.

One final entry for ACT 4.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED

He wrote:

An anomalous event can be detected before macroscopic consequence under at least some measured conditions.

Then:

A prospective model can make falsifiable predictions. One Geneva timing prediction failed. A second branch prediction succeeded within its frozen window.

Then:

Human intervention can causally modify local measured responses during an ongoing anomalous event.

Then:

Distributed local execution maintained a bounded internal region during severe external orientation deviation and one actuator-node loss.

Then:

No planetary implementation exists.

No portable implementation exists.

No universal cancellation law has been demonstrated.

Fundamental mechanism unknown.

He stopped.

The scientific summary.

Clean.

Bounded.

Below it:

WHAT HAS CHANGED

He thought longer.

Then wrote:

Before Geneva, the anomaly was a fact about nature.

Now control is a fact about us.

He stared at the sentence.

That one he kept.

Far below him, pumps moved helium through eleven healthy nodes and one isolated system under repair.

Every node possessed local authority.

Every node possessed limits.

Every node could refuse.

The architecture had survived because control was incomplete.

Ian understood that now.

Intellectually.

Even physically.

What he did not yet know was whether he could accept the same principle outside the machine.

A government could refuse.

A scientist could refuse.

An engineer could refuse.

Another country could act.

Another laboratory could build.

Another person could choose a different target state.

The thought sat badly.

Not because he believed he knew everything.

He no longer did.

Because for the first time, he knew enough to understand how dangerous control might become in someone else's hands.

He closed the notebook.

Through the glass, the twelve-node lattice remained still.

It could not choose what counted as protection.

It could not choose who deserved the safer side of a boundary.

It could not choose when an acceptable correction became a weapon.

Those decisions existed outside the equations.

And the equations would obey whoever supplied the target.

Ian stood there for a long time.

The first problem had been whether the anomaly was real.

The second had been whether it could be changed.

Both now had answers.

The next problem was harder.

Someone would have to decide what reality was allowed to become.


# EPILOGUE: THE OWNER OF THE BOUNDARY


## Opening Chapter

### Opening

*### [Scene 1: The Owner of the Boundary]*

Three months after Geneva, gravity had become boring again.

Rain fell vertically against the windows of the café.

Coffee remained at the bottom of cups.

A child's red balloon, tied to the back of a chair, pulled upward for reasons no one in the room considered remarkable.

Across the lake, a passenger aircraft descended toward Geneva Airport along a smooth conventional trajectory.

Ian Yoo watched it until the landing gear disappeared behind the buildings.

Nothing happened.

No discontinuity.

No change in apparent vertical.

No disagreement between where the aircraft was and where its clocks believed it to be.

It simply flew.

He had forgotten how strange that looked.

The café was crowded.

Students.

CERN engineers.

Tourists.

Two people arguing in French over a laptop.

A woman balancing three glasses on one hand.

No one tested the floor before stepping onto it.

No one checked whether the surface of their drink agreed with the building's structural frame.

The world had resumed spending certainty it had never actually possessed.

Ian understood why.

Civilization could not function otherwise.

You could not measure local vertical before every step.

You could not verify spatial connectivity before crossing a doorway.

You could not compare four clocks before boarding an aircraft.

At some point, physical regularity had to become habit.

That did not make it fundamental.

Only useful.

His tablet vibrated.

Sarah.

Where are you?

Ian typed:

Here.

Three dots appeared.

Then:

That is not a location.

He sent the café name.

Her response came immediately.

Vance is early.

Ian looked at the time.

He was twelve minutes early himself.

Then he can wait.

Sarah:

He says waiting compounds.

Ian closed the message.

Of course he did.

Geneva had not experienced another anomalous event.

Neither had Seoul.

The Pacific monitoring network had recorded several acoustic disturbances, all eventually attributable to ordinary causes.

Flight 702 had returned to service after months of inspection, software review, structural examination, and argument.

The aircraft had not teleported again.

No other aircraft had reproduced its event.

That absence had become evidence of nothing.

Correctly.

A-173 remained.

The astronomical residual persisted.

The pulsar-timing compatibility persisted.

The inward-moving model survived some new data and failed to sharpen under others.

No countdown appeared.

No front was observed approaching Earth.

No theory won.

The world had not ended.

Instead, it had started ordering equipment.

Major airports now preserved physically impossible GNSS updates instead of reducing them immediately to navigation faults.

Several high-rise regulators had issued interim guidance on multidirectional restraint and independent inertial sensing.

Deep-ocean observatories were adding raw timing channels to acoustic networks.

National metrology institutes had discovered that everyone suddenly wanted portable optical clocks.

Superconducting-conductor qualification slots that had once attracted niche interest now had waiting lists.

Three independent laboratories had received approval to replicate portions of the Denver effect.

None had yet reproduced the full macroscopic support result.

The Netherlands optical team had strengthened its propagation finding.

A Japanese group had reported a compatible low-amplitude phase response, then withdrawn part of its initial analysis after discovering a thermal cross-coupling term.

Sterling had called that good science.

The press had called it confusion.

Both descriptions were accurate.

There was still only one Geneva Distributed Cancellation Lattice.

Twelve physical nodes.

Eleven currently qualified for full operation.

Node Four had returned from repair eighteen days earlier but remained under restricted envelope pending repeated thermal cycling.

The system still occupied rooms.

Cryogenic plants.

Power infrastructure.

Timing infrastructure.

Service corridors.

People.

A field-control technology that required a facility the size of a research campus was difficult to steal in a briefcase.

For the moment.

Ian finished his coffee.

The surface remained horizontal.

He disliked noticing.

The meeting was in a private room on the third floor of a building owned by one of Vance's holding companies, far enough from CERN to avoid institutional symbolism and close enough that everyone could pretend the location had been chosen for convenience.

Sarah was already there.

Vance stood beside a wall display.

No title.

Only a world map.

Ian stopped.

Colored points covered North America, Europe, East Asia, India, and several other locations.

Some large.

Some small.

Some connected by lines.

He looked at Sarah.

"What is this?"

She closed her laptop.

"Ask him."

Vance turned.

"Programs."

One word.

Exactly as if that answered everything.

Ian stepped closer.

"Replication sites?"

"Some."

"Preparedness?"

"Some."

"Odysseus studies?"

"Some."

"National laboratories?"

"Mostly."

"Military?"

Vance paused.

"Some don't say."

Ian looked at the map again.

There were more points than he expected.

"Sources?"

"Public procurement."

"That's not enough for this."

"Industry inquiries."

"Which means?"

"Companies asking companies whether certain things can be manufactured."

"Private."

"Legally obtained."

"I didn't ask whether it was legal."

"I know."

Sarah stood.

"Don't assume every point is a field program."

"I'm not."

Ian zoomed into Japan.

One superconducting-magnet consortium.

One timing program.

One aerospace group.

The system connected them with a dotted line.

"Why are these linked?"

Vance answered:

"Personnel movement."

"That's speculation."

"Yes."

"Then don't show it as fact."

"Dotted."

Ian looked at him.

Vance sighed and opened the legend.

CONFIRMED PROGRAM

PROBABLE TECHNICAL PROGRAM

CAPABILITY CLUSTER

PROCUREMENT ANOMALY

UNKNOWN PURPOSE

Better.

Not good.

Better.

Ian moved to North America.

Two confirmed low-amplitude replication programs.

One defense laboratory with a broad advanced-field-control solicitation.

One aerospace contractor studying distributed timing and superconducting pulsed systems.

No explicit connection to Geneva.

No explicit need for one.

He looked at Europe.

Multiple civil programs.

One classified-looking gap where procurement data simply disappeared.

East Asia.

More.

India.

Growing.

No one had a Geneva-class system.

Not even close.

But the ingredients were moving.

Ian said:

"They don't have the full control basis."

"No," Vance said.

"They don't have our state-dependent kernel adaptation."

"No."

"Distributed natural-event fallback?"

"Not publicly."

"Node Seven fault data?"

Vance hesitated.

"Some probably do."

Ian turned.

"How?"

"I said probably."

"From whom?"

"I don't know."

"Then don't say it."

"Fine."

Vance looked back at the map.

"They don't have everything."

"No."

"They don't need everything."

Ian stared.

"To reproduce Geneva, they do."

"Today."

Vance enlarged a group of facilities.

High-field magnet laboratories.

Fusion programs.

Precision timing institutes.

Aerospace control teams.

Cryogenic engineering companies.

None had G-DCL.

Together they possessed most of its industrial vocabulary.

Vance said:

"They don't need your equations forever, Ian."

Ian said nothing.

"The first machine belongs to the people who understand the effect."

Vance pointed toward Geneva.

"The second belongs to the people who learn how to manufacture it."

Another set of points.

"The third belongs to whoever can deploy it."

Sarah looked at him.

"That's too neat."

"Probably."

"Reality isn't an investor deck."

"No."

Vance looked at Ian.

"But scaling has a direction."

Ian studied the map.

"How long?"

"For what?"

"A second high-amplitude system."

"I don't know."

"Estimate."

"No."

"You're Vance."

"Exactly."

Ian frowned.

Vance continued.

"A number would make you think time is the only variable."

"What else?"

"Access to conductor."

"Qualification."

"Control expertise."

"Cryogenics."

"Power density."

"Patents."

"Export rules."

"Classification."

"Politics."

He tapped the map.

"And whether someone decides they don't need to reproduce Geneva."

Ian looked at him.

"What does that mean?"

"They may build something worse."

Sarah opened another file.

The portable-module feasibility study.

Still no integrated prototype authorized.

Only components.

Compact power conversion.

smaller cryogenic systems.

high-temperature superconducting subassemblies.

local clocks.

radiation-qualified control hardware.

distributed safety architecture.

No vehicle-scale field module.

No high-amplitude directional experiment.

Not yet.

Ian read the latest status.

"They've added three more teams."

"Yes."

"Who approved that?"

"The steering group."

"Why?"

"Different hardware approaches."

"We don't need parallel miniaturization this early."

Sarah looked at him.

"Why not?"

"Because integration is already the risk."

"These aren't integrated."

"Eventually they will be."

"Probably."

"Then we should control the pace."

Sarah watched him.

There it was.

Again.

Ian noticed.

He stopped.

Vance did not.

"Slowing your program does not slow everyone else's."

Ian turned.

"That's not an argument to accelerate."

"No."

"It is always your argument."

"No."

Vance pointed at the map.

"This is my argument."

Dozens of points.

Most not under their authority.

Some not even known to be related.

Enough to make the uncertainty real.

Ian said:

"Then the international framework needs stronger restrictions."

Sarah leaned back against the table.

"On whom?"

"High-amplitude field research."

"Globally?"

"Yes."

"Under what authority?"

"The preparedness framework."

"It doesn't have that authority."

"Then give it authority."

"Countries won't."

"Then condition access to the Geneva data."

"Which data?"

"Control implementation."

"Already restricted."

"More."

Sarah was quiet.

Ian continued.

"Independent high-amplitude replication should require joint inspection."

"Require?"

"Yes."

"National programs too?"

"Especially national programs."

Vance looked at Sarah.

She did not react.

Ian said:

"No portable deployment outside international oversight."

Sarah asked:

"How?"

"Export controls."

"On what?"

"Critical actuator components."

"Which also support fusion."

"Then carve-outs."

"Timing hardware?"

"Control algorithms."

"Which can be re-derived."

"Not quickly."

"How quickly?"

Ian stopped.

He did not know.

Sarah asked:

"What exactly are you trying to control?"

"The technology."

"The machine?"

"The capability."

"Those aren't the same thing."

"Close enough."

"No."

Ian looked at her.

She continued.

"Control of the machine?"

"Yes."

"Control of the designs?"

"Yes."

"Control of manufacturing?"

"If necessary."

"Control of who researches it?"

Ian paused.

"High-risk work."

"Who defines high-risk?"

"We do."

The answer came too quickly.

Sarah's expression changed.

Not much.

Enough.

Ian heard it too.

He corrected.

"The international verification and safety boards."

"Better."

"But?"

Ian frowned.

"What?"

Sarah waited.

He understood.

"And technical leads."

"Which includes?"

"Me."

Silence.

Vance turned away from the screen.

Ian said:

"I'm not claiming ownership."

Sarah answered:

"I didn't say you were."

"This is responsibility."

"I know."

"Then why are you looking at me like that?"

"Because responsibility and ownership start sounding similar when the person responsible decides no one else can be trusted."

Ian stared.

"That's not fair."

"Probably not."

"You saw Geneva."

"Yes."

"You saw what one wrong phase reference did."

"Yes."

"You saw what centralized control almost did."

"Yes."

"You saw what happens if someone chooses the wrong target state."

"Yes."

"Then someone has to make sure they don't."

Sarah nodded.

"Yes."

Ian stopped.

That had been easier than expected.

Then she asked:

"Who?"

The room seemed quieter.

Ian looked at the map.

"People who understand the system."

"Technical qualification."

"Obviously."

"Scientific oversight."

"Yes."

"Safety authority."

"Yes."

"Governments."

"Some role."

"Public accountability."

"Yes."

"People inside the boundary."

Ian turned.

"What?"

Sarah pushed away from the table.

"You keep talking about who gets to operate the field."

"Yes."

"Who decides what it protects?"

"The operator."

"Exactly."

"That is what operators do."

Sarah shook her head.

"No."

She pointed toward the Geneva marker on the map.

"At NGC, the answer was easy."

"Why?"

"Empty test volume."

"Yes."

"Expensive equipment."

"Yes."

"Known boundary."

"Approximately."

"One facility."

"Yes."

She looked at him.

"Now move it."

Ian said nothing.

"A hospital."

"Protect the hospital."

"Whole building?"

"If possible."

"Generator?"

"Yes."

"Staff accommodation?"

"Maybe."

"Road outside?"

"Depends on scale."

"Neighboring building?"

"If possible."

"Which one?"

Ian frowned.

"That's implementation."

"No."

Sarah looked directly at him.

"That's ownership."

Vance said nothing.

For once.

Sarah continued.

"A boundary is not just a field solution."

Ian remembered writing almost the same thing.

A boundary is a decision.

She could not have seen the notebook.

"Someone decides what's inside."

"Yes."

"And what's outside."

"Yes."

"And when the two cannot both be protected?"

Ian looked away.

"Allocation."

Vance said the word quietly.

Sarah nodded.

Ian looked back at the map.

Cities.

Laboratories.

Countries.

Potential machines that did not yet exist.

He saw the problem.

That was not the same as accepting the conclusion.

"Then it needs governance before deployment."

Sarah nodded.

"Yes."

"Central standards."

"Yes."

"Common control limits."

"Yes."

"Independent veto."

"Yes."

"Mandatory verification."

"Yes."

"Restrictions on unilateral use."

"Probably."

Ian looked at her.

"So we agree."

"On rules."

"What don't we agree on?"

Sarah paused.

"Whether the rules exist to make sure no one owns the boundary."

Ian waited.

"Or to make sure the right people do."

Vance finally spoke.

"That's not a distinction governments enjoy."

Ian looked at him.

"No one asked you."

"No."

Vance walked toward the map.

"But that's why this matters."

He turned off the procurement layer.

The map became simpler.

Only confirmed and probable programs remained.

Still too many.

"The technology isn't dangerous because one person can own it today."

He pointed toward Geneva.

"They can't."

Then the other points.

"It's dangerous because eventually several people can."

Ian said:

"Then the safest architecture has to become the standard first."

Vance nodded.

"That I agree with."

"Local veto."

"Yes."

"Independent clocks."

"Yes."

"Fail silent."

"Yes."

"Restricted high-gradient modes."

"Maybe."

"Physical limitations against directional amplification."

"If possible."

"International audit."

"Good luck."

Ian glared.

Vance shrugged.

"Still worth doing."

Sarah closed the map.

"That's enough."

Ian looked at her.

"We haven't decided anything."

"We weren't going to."

"Then why meet?"

"To see what exists."

"That's not enough."

"No."

She gathered her things.

Ian watched.

"Where are you going?"

"CERN."

"For what?"

"Node Four thermal-cycle review."

"That's Aris."

"And verification."

Ian looked at the blank display.

"Sarah."

She stopped.

"What?"

"If other programs build without these safeguards?"

"We adapt."

"After?"

"Maybe."

"That's not acceptable."

"No."

"Then why are you comfortable with it?"

"I'm not."

She looked at him.

"I just don't think discomfort gives us jurisdiction over everyone else."

Ian said:

"If one of them weaponizes it—"

"We deal with it."

"Too late."

"Maybe."

"If they build a mobile directional field—"

"We deal with it."

"After deployment."

"Maybe."

"If they put a boundary around something we need to observe?"

Sarah looked at him.

"Then we learn what we can still observe."

"That's not an answer."

"It is."

"No."

"It's just one you don't like."

Ian stared at her.

Sarah softened slightly.

Not much.

"You learned to say I don't know."

"I still can."

"I know."

"Then what's your point?"

"That saying it isn't the end of the lesson."

Ian waited.

"Sometimes the next sentence is and someone else gets to decide."

He felt the resistance immediately.

"Not if they're unqualified."

"Sometimes they will be."

"Not if the risk is global."

"Who defines global?"

"We have events across three continents and an ocean."

"That's not what I asked."

Ian stopped.

Sarah continued.

"You cannot solve every dangerous uncertainty by moving the decision closer to yourself."

"I didn't say myself."

"No."

She looked at him for another second.

"Not yet."

Then left.

The door closed.

Ian looked at Vance.

"Say nothing."

Vance raised both hands.

"I was leaving."

"Good."

He walked toward the door.

Then stopped.

Ian closed his eyes.

"Of course."

Vance looked back.

"One thing."

"No."

"The programs on that map don't need to be malicious."

Ian opened his eyes.

"I know."

"No, you keep thinking about weapons."

"They matter."

"Yes."

Vance returned to the table.

"The harder problem is legitimate use."

Ian frowned.

"Explain."

"Suppose there are three operational systems."

"Fine."

"One anomaly."

"Where?"

"Doesn't matter."

"It matters completely."

"Exactly."

Vance nodded.

"City A has twenty million people."

Ian waited.

"City B has the only manufacturing plant for critical node hardware."

"Yes."

"Site C is a military early-warning network."

"Stop."

"Why?"

"Because it's arbitrary."

"Allocation problems always are until they aren't."

Ian stared.

Vance continued.

"Who gets the machine?"

"Depends on event geometry."

"Good."

"Control range."

"Good."

"Evacuation alternatives."

"Good."

"Probability of success."

"Good."

"Population."

"Good."

"Strategic importance."

Ian stopped.

Vance smiled without humor.

"There."

"That's politics."

"Yes."

"Then politicians decide."

"Probably."

"With technical advice."

"Hopefully."

"That's normal."

"Exactly."

Ian looked at him.

"Then what's your point?"

Vance picked up his coat.

"You're going to hate normal."

He left.

Ian remained in the room for another twenty minutes.

The map was off.

He could still see it.

Points across the world.

Programs.

Not machines.

Not yet.

The distinction mattered.

For how long, he did not know.

His phone vibrated.

A message from Seo-yeon.

Are you still in Geneva next week?

He looked at it.

Then replied.

Yes.

Her response:

Good. I found something of yours while moving boxes.

A photograph followed.

A small drafting compass lay on an old dining table.

Silver-colored steel.

Worn hinge.

One pointed leg.

One graphite holder.

Ian stared.

He had believed it was still in storage in London.

Apparently not.

Bring it, he wrote.

Seo-yeon replied:

You told me years ago it was useless.

Ian looked at the image.

I was wrong.

There was a long pause.

Then:

About the compass?

Ian almost smiled.

He did not answer.

Six days later, rain came to Geneva.

Not anomalous.

Cold autumn rain.

It fell from low gray clouds and struck the lake in thousands of small impacts that no monitoring network classified as significant.

Seo-yeon had sent the compass by insured courier after refusing to trust Ian with remembering to collect it.

The case sat in his coat pocket.

He walked alone along the lake after sunset.

No meeting.

No alert.

No instrumentation.

For once, no one needed anything from him.

The city lights stretched across wet pavement.

People moved under umbrellas.

A tram passed behind him.

Its steel wheels followed rails.

Its weight followed gravity.

Its position followed a continuous path.

Ordinary things.

He had spent years trying to find variables institutions could not rewrite.

Now he understood the darker version of that ambition.

A physical law did not need to lie to become political.

It only needed an actuator.

He stopped near an empty bench.

The rain had weakened.

He took the compass from his pocket.

The metal was colder than he expected.

His father's hand had polished parts of it smooth decades ago.

Ian remembered graphite on paper.

A dining table in Seoul.

Seventeen years old.

The confidence of someone who believed the greatest difficulty in drawing a circle was choosing the correct center.

Set the center before you draw, Ian.

He opened the compass.

The hinge resisted slightly.

Then moved.

He had no paper.

Only the wet wooden bench.

He placed the pointed leg lightly against the surface anyway.

Did not scratch it.

The other leg hovered several centimeters away.

Center.

Radius.

Boundary.

Three things that had once seemed mathematically innocent.

The center defined the circle.

The radius defined what belonged within it.

Nothing in the geometry explained why that region should matter.

Humans supplied that part.

His father had said:

If you keep moving the center every time the line becomes inconvenient, the circle means nothing.

Ian had spent years hearing only the first half of the lesson.

Fix the center.

Do not move it.

One reality.

One realized state.

One structure beneath uncertainty.

Then Geneva had forced another truth on him.

A center could be fixed and still not be knowable from everywhere in time.

The machine had survived because no controller was allowed to pretend otherwise.

Twelve nodes.

Twelve clocks.

Local authority.

Bounded disagreement.

No instantaneous owner of the whole state.

He understood that now.

The physics did not offend him anymore.

Not in the same way.

He moved the graphite leg through the air.

An invisible circle around the point.

Whoever chose the center chose the boundary.

Whoever chose the boundary chose what remained inside.

A collider.

A hospital.

A city.

A government.

A military installation.

A data center.

A person.

Protection required a protected set.

There was no equation that made that choice morally neutral.

Sarah's question returned.

Who decides what's inside the boundary, Ian?

He had no answer.

Not a complete one.

Perhaps there was no complete answer.

That no longer frightened him in the way it once had.

He could live with incomplete explanation.

He had learned that much.

The anomaly's cause remained unknown.

A-173 remained unresolved.

Flight 702 still had no conventional path.

The Pacific still had no accepted mechanism.

Seoul had no fundamental model.

And yet they had acted.

Measured.

Failed.

Acted again.

Learned.

The absence of certainty no longer felt like an accusation.

What he could not accept was the map.

Not the uncertainty of it.

The distribution.

Programs he could not inspect.

Engineers he did not know.

Governments with different thresholds.

Laboratories that might decide local veto was inefficient.

Procurement officers who might prefer one powerful node to twelve disagreeable ones.

Designers who might see Node Seven's failure trace not as a warning, but as a capability.

Someone would eventually realize that a field designed to keep vertical from rotating could also be used to rotate it.

Someone would decide that fail-silent wasted available energy.

Someone would override a margin because the simulation looked convincing.

Someone would build the wrong machine beautifully.

The rain intensified slightly.

Drops struck the compass.

Ian closed it halfway.

His father's second lesson returned.

You don't fix the evidence.

He had learned that too.

Sterling had forced him.

Sarah had forced him harder.

Failed predictions remained failed.

Contaminated channels remained contaminated.

An observation did not become stronger because the world needed reassurance.

Truth was not control.

He understood the difference now.

But knowledge changed responsibility.

That was the part Sarah treated too lightly.

Or perhaps he thought she did.

If you knew a system could fail in a particular way, you could not stand aside and call the outcome someone else's choice.

If you knew centralized fast control was dangerous, you had to prevent it.

If you knew a high-gradient mode could become a weapon, you had to restrict it.

If you knew another group was building without the right safeguards—

You had to act before the mistake became irreversible.

Didn't you?

He looked across the lake.

No answer came.

Only rain.

He thought of Sterling.

The problem is who you mean by we.

Ian had no satisfying response.

International boards could fail.

Governments could fail.

Markets could fail.

Scientists could fail.

He could fail.

Geneva had proven that repeatedly.

That did not make all failures equivalent.

Some people knew more.

Some systems were better designed.

Some choices were more defensible than others.

Humility did not require pretending expertise was meaningless.

Uncertainty did not require surrendering judgment.

The argument assembled itself carefully.

Almost beautifully.

No one should own the boundary.

Therefore no single government should control it.

No company.

No military.

No laboratory.

No individual.

Good.

Then the next step.

Someone had to prevent unilateral ownership.

Someone had to preserve the distributed architecture.

Someone had to keep the safety rules ahead of deployment.

Someone had to know when another program was about to remove them.

Someone had to remain technically ahead long enough to make the safer design the standard.

Not forever.

Only until the institutions were strong enough.

Only until the technology matured.

Only until the world understood what it held.

Ian recognized the shape of the reasoning.

That did not make it wrong.

A dangerous argument could still be correct.

He told himself that.

He opened the compass fully.

Point.

Radius.

Boundary.

His father had told him to set the center before drawing.

At seventeen, Ian had believed the center was something reality provided.

At Geneva, he had learned that control required choosing one.

That was different.

And much more dangerous.

He touched the steel point to the wet wood.

Very lightly.

No mark.

The graphite leg traced an invisible arc.

Half a circle.

Then stopped.

He imagined the world map.

Geneva.

Denver.

Seoul.

The Pacific.

The Atlantic.

A-173 somewhere beyond immediate human reach.

Then the new points.

Programs.

Factories.

Laboratories.

Future nodes.

Future boundaries.

No one owned them yet.

Not completely.

The equations would spread.

The hardware would shrink.

The boundaries would move.

Someone would choose where they stopped.

Ian closed the compass.

The dangerous variable was no longer the geometry.

It was the hand that chose the center.

He looked across the dark water and knew, with a certainty he no longer mistook for proof, what he would do next.

I must control it.


# APPENDIX


## Appendix A: Glossary of Terminology

### Opening

**Tensor Fluid (텐서 유체)**

The conceptualization of the vacuum of space not as an empty void, but as a compressible, dynamic fluid governed by complex topological and hydrodynamic principles.

**Cosmic Shear / Phase-Transition Wave (우주적 전단 / 상전이 파동)**

A macroscopic topological fracture propagating through the spatial metric, capable of unzipping the local geometry of the universe and altering the fundamental constants of gravity and distance.

**Matched Singularity Cancellation / Exact Cancellation (정합 특이점 상쇄 / 완전 상쇄)**

A topological regularization technique pioneered by Ian Yoo. It involves generating an artificial, opposing geometric phase rotation ($C_s$) to perfectly match the singular geometry of a collapsing spatial defect ($Q_s$), thereby algebraically neutralizing the divergence before the physical limit is reached.

**Epsilon Regularization (엡실론 정규화)**

An orthodox, mathematically conservative patch championed by Professor Arthur Sterling. It utilizes an arbitrary scalar constant ($\epsilon$) to artificially cap unphysical infinities in effective field models, effectively hiding underlying structural flaws in the spatial metric.

**Comoving Metric Neighborhood (동행 계량 이웃)**

A localized bubble of spacetime that translates cohesively across macroscopic distances. Objects within this bubble preserve their internal inertial reference frames and experience zero acceleration or kinetic friction, despite bypassing vast Euclidean distances.

**Standing Wave Node (정상파 마디)**

A localized coordinate within the tensor fluid experiencing destructive interference, where the vibrational amplitude drops to zero. This effectively nullifies standard gravitational vectors, allowing matter to decouple from planetary mass.

## Appendix B: Key Governing Equations

### Opening

**1. Matched Singularity Cancellation Limit (정합 특이점 상쇄 극한)**

The fundamental algebraic principle of neutralizing a spatial tear by matching its divergent geometry:

$$ \lim_{r \to 0} [Q_s(r) + C_s(r)] = q_0 + c_0 \rightarrow 0 $$

**2. Tensor Fluid Continuity Equation (텐서 유체 연속 방정식)**

Adapted from classical hydrodynamics, defining the conservation of mass-energy within the compressible spatial vacuum:

$$ \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho v) = 0 $$

**3. Topological Phase Rotation (위상학적 위상 회전)**

The quantum geometric rotation induced to manipulate the local tensor field:

$$ S = \hbar\theta $$

**4. Bianchi Identities & Conservation (비앙키 항등식 및 보존칙)**

The geometric constraint demanding that the stress-energy tensor remains locally conserved, ensuring that topological energy cannot be administratively deleted:

$$ \nabla_\mu \tilde{V}^{\mu\nu} = 0 $$
